I don't see any symbolism though--people suck, rational thought is never given the respect it deserves, and as someone who wears glasses I dread the thought of being in a survival situation. (Also afraid if I ever get mugged or otherwise assaulted that I'll end up with a shard of glass in my eyeball. Poor vision is fun you guys.) How is any of that revelatory? Maybe it's just that I'm reading it in 2017 USA where the social order is collapsing before our eyes anyway. Maybe this was a shocking reminder of humanity's animal instincts in 1950s Britain. Idk. 
 Glad to say I finally read it though. It's one of those books that it seems like everyone else read in high school but was never assigned to us. And I did love the cover and the size of this edition. It's perfectly hand-sized.

I started reading this at 8PM last night and just finished now, about 1 pm. The rate at which I read this should be an indicator of my feelings about it. 
 This book and I got off to a great start--it made me laugh on page 2 and I quickly decided it was wonderful, mostly 'cause the narrator was sassy and amusing. I was already mentally planning on giving it five stars from pretty early on, but after the protag's relationship with Lend progresses and it turns out he's nice and relatively normal,  a lot of the suspense dropped out of the story for me. While I find their developing relationship interesting enough to read about it didn't quite have that pull of when Lend first showed up and was an enigma. But soon enough the rest of the plot starts to fall into place and more mysteries arise, so I was... re-engaged? Is that a word? 
 A few minor criticisms: 
 Evie's introduction to the idea that paranormals don't need to be tagged and monitored is a bit rushed and introduced a bit quickly and bluntly. It doesn't feel like she comes to learn this over time, organically. It was a bit too fast to change her mind about something she'd spent so long believing and even perpetuating. 
 I kept forgetting about Lish. I think Evie didn't really grieve  enough--she seemed pretty happy considering she'd lost someone who was supposedly her best friend for a long time.  It didn't feel quite right. Maybe we the readers never got to connect with Lish quite enough to mourn her, too.  
 I can't disagree with others' reviews saying the main character is a bit too perfect. And while I couldn't exactly relate to her extreme exaggerated stereotypical girlishness, I still found her interesting enough to continue reading about. 
 Despite a few flaws I ultimately enjoyed this book quite a bit, so it gets a solid 4 stars from me.

Animal Farm seems like a book for kids. A person may think it's a classic children's book about a jolly pig that lives on a farm. It even looks like it'll be a funny book with a 'happily-ever-after' or a nice ending. I find it exceptional that all of the ideas I would have thought you had after seeing the book's cover is the exact opposite of the book when you read it. 
 Animal Farm is an extraordinary illuminating fable for all times. 
 Since its publication at the end of World War II, it became a sensational star-book which was read by millions of people around the world. According to George Orwell (Eric Blair) when he mentioned the words 'We were very lucky to get out of Spain alive", he was not talking about his experiences during the Spanish Civil War, which he described in another novel Homage to Catalonia in 1938 but about the murderous political agendas of Stalin in 1937. In Animal Farm, he described how escaping the communist in Spain taught him how easily covert tyrannical ways can control people in a democratic country. This had motivated George Orwell to be a devoted Democratic Socialist. 
 The novel started with an Old Boar in a certain farm in England scheming a plan to revolt against the human. And when the animals of the farm successfully revolted against its human lord, they didn't expect to slide into a more brutal tyranny amongst themselves. 
 "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others" 
 George Orwell effectively showed the readers how the animals was played out through deception, cruelty and the two-facedness (hypocrisy) by an unruly leader. It is also ironic that at the end of the novel, one cannot tell the difference of a fat and hungry pig's face from a human. 
 P.S: I had to hide this from my dad when I was reading this novel. He said I should start comprehending my law books (which I did..or did I? hoho) and stop reading SOME (take note of the emphasis.haha) books. Well, I say Animal Farm is not just some book. hoho. (Don't worry I won't start my own revolution. what? haha!).

I've been longing for an epic modernised retelling of Little Red Riding Hood for some time now, yet I oddly did not expect to find it in part 2 of The Lunar Chronicles: 'Scarlet' (even though it's very obviously based on said fairytale). Well, Marissa Meyer ... consider my longing fulfilled! 
 In my opinion, it's quite rare for the second part of a trilogy to outshine the first. With Scarlet, this is exactly so. Seen as how I gave 'Cinder' 4 stars back in the day, it seemed only fitting to give Scarlet 5. Why? The stakes are higher, the new characters are wonderful and ... (new fictional crush alert) Wolf. * sigh * 
 Scarlet and Wolf were adorable together from the first second they crossed paths. Wolf actually reminds me SO much of an OC of mine, so of course I loved him straight off the bat: his appetite (tomatoes!), his eyes, his protectiveness ... 
 His dynamic with Scarlet is perfectly written and I couldn't help falling in love with Wolf in Scarlet's stead (before she consciously does too, that is). The electricity crackled of the pages between the fiery redhead and demure yet dangerous wolf. I loved every second of it, but if I had to pick a favorite Scar+Wolf moment ... 
 ... [SPOILER] That scene were he kisses her in her prison cell to give her the ID chip was a stroke of sheer brilliance on Marissa Meyer's part, if you ask me. It's one of those scenes that'll haunt and taunt me with an everlasting "Why couldn't you have written that?". It was so unexpected but so so right. A punch in the gut you happily take.[END OF SPOILER] 
 But 'Scarlet' is not all about Scarlet and Wolf, of course. Cinder's story continues in 'Scarlet' when she escapes from prison with a new ally at her side: Captain Thorne. Thorne was one of those amazingly alive characters who are flawed and charming and unforgettable all at once. And I was glad to have Iko back too! Her complaining about her spaceship-size was very amusing. 
 The Kai chapters were a bit less interesting to me, but necessary to the story, so I understand why they were needed. All in all Scarlet was everything I wanted from a modernised Red Riding Hood and MORE: well-crafted, well-written and surprisingly romantic. 
 The Lunar Chronicles are something quite special ...

Dystopic sci-fi/speculative near future fiction that explores the dark days ahead if when the world inevitably faces a fresh water crisis. I loved the pace and the grittiness of The Water Knife. I didn't so much love the machismo and Bacigalupi's apparent complete lack of understanding when it comes to writing female characters (particularly female characters who have just been tortured and threatened with sexual violence who would MOST DEFINITELY NOT want to have sex with the next man they saw, wounds still fresh, even if that man killed her assailants). That aside, the tension, pace, and conspiracy in this story were on point. Some of the details were a little fuzzy and probably wouldn't hold up to close scrutiny, but that's sci-fi, you gotta give a little to get a little. As some major ecological crisis like this seems unavoidable for us now, at some point in the future, this type of speculative fiction takes on an even more unsettling tone. And of course, I love me a good open ending. I, for one, am hoping Bacigalupi comes back to this and explores what exactly goes down around the Great Lakes, because you know we're not giving up our Lake Michigan water.

This wasn't my favorite of her books, but I enjoyed it. Maya's character was a lot of fun. She wants nothing more than to be a musician. She's in a band, has a quasi-boyfriend, life is good. Then all in a matter of days, it all comes crashing down. The guy she's been hooking up with ditches her for her band mate. The band she started kicks her out. To make matters worse, she is forced to spend her Senior Shadow Day following around a young country music star. He is so not her type and his music is the last kind of music she is interested in. Jesse is not exactly friendly either. To say he is guarded is an understatement. He doesn't trust people, for good reason, and from the get go he tests her and pushes her away. Throughout the day, something changes. He starts to realize that perhaps she isn't just after something from him. Perhaps she is exactly the person he needs by his side. For her, the day begins to be less painful and turns out to be perhaps the best day ever. Jesse just might be the person to help her get over her fear of the solo and strike out on her own. One day may just change both of their lives. It was a fun book and a fun romance. Not a lot to it, but overall enjoyable.

Crash has been on my TBR shelf for a good long while now. I thought the synopsis sounded like it could be interesting and the cover kind of intrigued me - except for the super arched eyebrow which kind of bugs me. But that could just be bitterness over my own need of frequent brow waxes... 
 So our main character is 16-year-old Jules, whose family-run pizza place is in the midst of a fierce rivalry with another pizza place that just happens to be owned by the family of her crush (or in 16-year-old speak: the great love of her life), Sawyer. So there's the whole Romeo and Juliet vibe going on. Things get even more complicated when Jules starts to have increasingly frequent visions of a car crash and Sawyer is one of the victims. 
 What is Jules to do? I get that this is the central plot for the book, but there's just soooooo much time spent with Jules watching and re-watching the vision (she sees it on billboards, in reflections and on the tv or computer...). There's a lot of contemplating whether or not she's gone crazy. There is just not a lot that happens in the book outside of Jules' head and vision. 
 While Jules was a pretty well-developed character, I didn't find her all that likable. I did enjoy her close relationship with her siblings, especially her brother Trey. I liked Sawyer, but he could've been a little more developed. He hadn't talked to Jules in years and his big turnaround towards the end of the book seemed a little bit forced. 
 While Jules ultimately figures out how to understand and deal with the vision (yay!), it's never explained why she has it. Does it run in the family? Is she psychic? Will it happen to her again? There is a twist at the end that I found interesting and will carry those questions into the next book in the series. 
 Overall, Crash was ok for me. It's short chapters made it easy to read and the mystery was enough to keep me turning the page. I'm interested enough to read the rest of the series, but not interested enough that I'll be doing it any time soon.

Very entertaining and full of chuckles read with a light touch of medical kink. 
 The Trouble with Tony really is a fun read. In this story we have Tony DiMarco who used to be a Seattle PD detective but after getting shot in the leg quit the police and became a private investigator. He has been hired by a family to investigate the death of their 28 year old daughter. As part of this investigation Tony is led to the "Expanding Horizons" sex clinic where the victim was undergoing treatment. 
 Tony first visits the clinic under the pretense that he is a sex addict but after meeting take-no-bullshit Dr. Jack Halloran he quickly fesses up to his real affliction. Dr. Jack Halloran used to be an Army surgeon but after being injured in the line of fire he can no longer perform surgery. So he had to quit the service and find a new career. This is how he came to be a sex counselor at this clinic. He feels damaged and only a reflection of who he used to be. 
 This story is chock-full of sexual euphemisms. Plus even though Tony's very stereotypical Italian family lives across the U.S. (particularly his mom,) it is a source of hilarious dialogue. What I liked about this book is that even though it is a short story, it has a nice plot and the characters are three dimensional. I look forward to reading the next installment.

This is a very emotional story. It deals with rape by a close family friend. Although there are details, the author handles it very well. I suggest you do not read this or skip over the details if rape is a trigger for you. 
 This is Beth's story of pain and rebirth! Rebirth. This is the only word that I can think to describe Beth. She is reborn by the end of the book, thanks to her loyal family and the ones that love her.  Hard as it was to actually trust people again, she did and finds out not everyone wants to use her.  
 So many years she had to step outside herself and not be present in her mind, just to get through her life until she can't take it anymore. What happens after, some would say may be just as bad as the first betrayal.....this time by her parents. 
 At 14 and having no support at home, she goes to live with her grandparents where she begins to heal. She has to heal all the way around before she can take down her walls. With the help of some very special people she begins that process, until life throws her a few more curveballs and fastpitches before it allows her to finally have her happy ending. 
 This book really brought me in with the first few chapters, which rarely happens lately. The key to a good book is for an attention grabber in the first few chapters. The Final Piece definitely did that. I cared about Beth and wanted to protect her and I loved Ryan for all his amazing qualities. The authors words make you want to keep going even though Beth's life is hard to read about. You want to scream and tell her whats best for her; tell her to stay and hang on. Over all this story was entertaining, well written, and kept my attention through the whole book. There wasn't a time where I wanted to move on. I was invested in this book and the characters.

Several folks have reviewed this favorably. I'll give Mr. Wynne-Jones credit for a multiple-perspective work that incorporates 3rd person and 2nd person narratives. The 2nd person section - Blink's - was hard for me to sink into, and perhaps alternating it with Caution's made both characters more remote. Both teens have stories and secrets, and by the end of the story everything turns out alright. 
 But what teen will really enjoy this? I can't see her or him in my minds eye. The gritty-living-on-the-streets part ends and then isn't revisited, the love-story takes too long to get going, only to not really sizzle, the what-is-going-on-in-the-woods-mystery is never made clear. The whole thing just seemed like a mess.

Summary: Harry Potter is back for his fourth year at Hogwarts. During the summer, Ron's family has invited him and Hermione to see the Quidditch World Cup. During the games, the dark mark is seen in the sky and the games end early. At school they learn that Hogwarts will be hosting the Triwizard Tournament, where three students are chosen to participate. Two other wizarding schools are invited, Beauxbatons, an all female school, and Durmstrang, and an all boy's school. This year, 4 students are picked to participant, and of course Harry is one of them. 
 My thoughts: I enjoyed how this book still included Voldemort, yet the majority of the adventure related around the Triwizard Tournament. A larger book then the last 3, the three tasks were very well described, and throughout the challenges I constantly cheered and recoiled hoping all the characters would be okay. 
 With the progression of the stories, you can see J.K. Rowlings writing improved and her stories getting darker. I love how this progression also relates to the growth of the characters and the hardships they have to endure along the way. We can see how this book is darker than the others, considering that one character dies in this novel. Hogwarts is now, not as safe as it used to be and Harry and his classmates are not impervious to harm. 
 Quote p.173: "Harry put his Omnioculars to his eyes again. It was hard to see what was happening below, because leprechauns were zooming delightedly all over the field, but he could just make out Krum, surrounded by mediwizards. He looked surlier than ever and refused to let them mop him up. His team members were around him, shaking their heads and looking dejected; a short way away, the Irish players were dancing gleefully in a shower of gold descending from their mascots."
Another great, vivid, suspenseful novel by Mr King. Sequel to Mr. Murder, and I thought this book was a bit better.

 I can't really say this is appreciably better than Fool Moon. Everyone said it was, but now I'm beginning to fear all of my friends are compulsive liars. Or maybe perpetrating a long joke at my expense. The world will never know. 
 For a while this book threw me off. The introduction of Michael (a character I rather liked by the way) is done in such a way as I was worried I'd skipped a book accidentally. He's tossed in as though we've already met him, and I found it a touch jarring. Especially since every time Harry talks about his basement apartment - or his girlfriend Susan, or his car the Blue Beetle, or Bob, or his damn cat - he has to give us the backstory on them again as though we haven't read the previous books. 
 Similarly, all the stuff with Kravos felt like I should've known that already, that I had missed something. An interim book or short story perhaps. By the time the dream sequence comes explaining that, it felt way too late. That feeling resolves itself by the end of the novel, but by then it was too late. 
 Again we fall into the same pattern of Harry spending most of the book half dead, with him miraculously finding that last bit of strength he needs to pull things off. It's like watching Dragon Ball Z again, Harry gets beaten to where he looks like he'll surely lose, taps into that secret inner strength or whatever, and then burns everything the fuck down. He never seems to win by being smarter, or better than his adversaries - he just gets pissed and starts fires. It all gets to feeling a bit repetitive. 
 Again, too, I'd like to note the misogyny. 
 I am not saying Jim Butcher is necessarily misogynist, to be clear. I don't believe authors who write about murderers are also murderers either. Harry, though, has some problems. 
 Nearly every single woman, with the possible exception of Michael's wife Charity, is described in an overly sexualized manner. If I have to read another description of a female character that details how her clothes cup her breasts or how her nipples poke out I am going to jam a fork into thigh. Seriously, with the exception of Thomas - who is intended to be a hyper-sexualized male character - no male gets that treatment. Harry describes Morgan as looking like Sean Connery, talks about his ponytail, etc. If he treated him like every female character it'd be more like: 
 Then Morgan stepped out of the woods. His taut shoulders stretched the fabric of his shirt to its limit. The dark jeans he wore clung to his legs, accentuating his firm, shapely ass. I couldn't help but notice the bulge in the front of his pants. Someone was happy to see me. 
 If you are a guy, and that is weird to you, please recognize that is how it comes across to women. If you are an author and your character is not a thirteen year old boy or a recovering nymphomaniac, having them describe people like that gets really tiresome. 
 Hopefully the next one gets better like everyone says - though now I'm concerned it won't live up to the hype.

Lately, a lot of the books I've been reading seem overwritten, with an adjective (or two!) hanging off every noun. In that sea of verbiage, it's a relief to find McCarthy's clean, sharp prose with hardly a modifier. His keen ear for dialogue lends plenty of color that might otherwise be missing, and mostly the story is as taut as the prose. 
 Perhaps a drawback to this writing style, though, is the opacity of the characters. We don't get any glimpses inside the most intriguing characters, and spend too much time inside the head of the local sheriff who, despite all the first-person narrative, plays more like a stock character than a three-dimensional presence. Though McCarthy feints at complicating the sheriff a bit at the end, you won't need to worry about identifying "bad guy" and "good guy," it's all spelled out, they're practically wearing white hats and black hats (cowboy, of course). I can see why McCarthy's books are so readily adapted to the screen as they can feel more reported than written, with lots of room for the director and the actors to interpret everything besides the action. 
 But perhaps I don't give McCarthy enough credit. There's an inevitability about the story that, after all, wasn't inevitable at all, but only seems so because he crafted and wrote it so well. It's like a machine that works so well and simply, you don't even spare a thought to the engineer who built it. He's written the sleekest crime thriller ever with nothing extraneous in the way of information, plot twists, character, etc. He sets up a situation, pushes certain characters into play, and off it goes, winding down to the end. I think Henry James said that character is plot, and, in this book at least, McCarthy seems to agree. 
 Even for all my quibbling, though, I did enjoy the book and found it difficult to put down. I look forward to reading _The Road_, and might even give the Border Trilogy a reconsideration.

 What this book excels at: sense of place, and sense of horror. In those regards it's its own vivid world. Probably the most chilling moments came near the end, when the General hides in his daughter's wardrobe one night and sees Carmilla/Millarca creeping into the room, and then the scene where the hunting party unearths Camilla's tomb. What they see there is truly chilling.  
 What this book does not excel at: character development. The author is lazy and just informs the reader in a brief summary that Carmilla and the main character, Laura, are now very close friends (probably more). We as readers are often very distant from that relationship. But in fact, all the characters are just like pieces on a chessboard, moved around for the sake of plot. There's really very little attempt to humanize most of them, and disappointingly, the only area in which the author is thorough in his development is physical appearance and mannerisms. The fact that I didn't know these characters by the book's end killed almost all my enthusiasm for the book. 
 Another complaint I have is that it's repetitive or irrelevant in places. But I'll counter that with why I'm glad I read it: it's the father (mother?) of the vampire genre, and it's fascinating to see those ideas coming together, and to think how this type of story has changed over more than a century of reimaginings. That historical and literary interest, paired with the lush setting and the skillful horror scenes, are this novella's redeeming qualities.

Fangirl is about a girl named Cath who is a fangirl over Simon Snow. Not only is she a fan and have multiple posters and shirts about the books, she also writes her own fanfics. Cath used to do this with her twin Wren but, the two are on the rocks ever since Wren wanted to branch out and not be roommates for their first year at university. 
 So, Cath has to learn how to live without relying on her twin, and figure out how to live with her anxiety, which isn't easy with all the newness through at her. 
 I went into this book prepared not to like it because of reviews but, I did- like it. I'm not in love nor do I think I'll ever re-read it but, it was nice to connect to a protagonist so strongly yet, it was scary and uncomfortable. Her difficult time with eating alone, or going to class, even with dealing with a roommate, I understood her. And while we see the anxiety bring her down there are times when she is VERY strong and brave which I don't think are truly given the magnitude of attention they should be given or perhaps things had to be written a certain way for the story to progress. 
 As any writer of fanfic can tell you, finding time to write between school, hanging with friends, especially when you have a significant other, really brings the writing time to nil. The fact she was able to find time is astounding to me-- then again... Freshman. I'd bet after she finishs Carry On she stops or barely writes. 
 So, it was nice to read about someone who could understand what I've been through. 
 Cath was hard to be around sometimes but, I liked her as a main character and I'm happy to have read her story. Love it? Nah, Really Liked it? Possibly but I think it hit too close to home sometimes yet, other times Cath didn't make sense... But, I enjoyed the book and would definitely recommend it to some of my fanfic writing/fangirl friends.

I liked the question of whether or not the stuff going on in our heads is as real as what goes on outside of it. I could see this culture bleeding into other science fiction realms where the authors put forth the idea that entire civilizations will decide to go purely digital and abandon the real world except to protect their planet as best they can before disappearing into their computers. 
 The execution of the series however just kept going down. It drifted farther away from the brother and sister (who also drifted away from each other) and towards the super religious fucked up character Marcus. Who builds entire towers of religion-based hatred and uses them to excuse whatever he wants to do (kill everyone he thinks isn't human anymore (because he's an asshole)). 
 Now I do like how Bertauski showed how scared the general populous was with all the changes going on. It felt very believable. However. What his main characters kept getting up to inalienated me until I finally started skimming through what was going on and by the start of the third book ended up quitting entirely. My prescription to them? Therapy. Lots of it.

I'm still debating between 1 or 2 stars for this. I was so incredibly disappointed with this that I'm kind of leaning toward 1 star, but if I'm being fair there were enough parts of it that I liked to warrant another star.

In an upper-middle class suburban area with plenty of rich parents. Actually, most of the people who live in my area work in the entertainment business in one way or another and just commute to LA, since I only live an hour away. Half the people there think they're genius DJs. Their parents have money to buy the most expensive equipment and private lessons with the guy that taught Jimi Hendrix how to play. 
 Okay, maybe that's extreme, but my point is a girl playing an acoustic guitar isn't all that impressive. Especially considering how two-dimensional all the characters were, I'd expect them to need a lot more before they got riled up. 
 None of that was enough to make me dislike the book, though. What really did it for me was miss Molly and her idiotic thinking and her idiotic actions. Here are my status updates to give you an idea: 
 10.0%: "So in 40 pages she's decided to join a bunch of guys she's just met swimming and wearing their clothes, gotten almost completely naked, and apparently gets all hot and bothered anytime two of them come near her even though one supposedly hates her guts.... sounds like all my first dates"

 "Thanks, Viktor. But hey, let's not allow that tool to ruin our day. It's over. So, you drive, huh?"

 _______________________________________________________________________

 Molly: "I love you." 
 Victor: "I'll just move out of the way so you can be with Weston." 
 Victor: "I can't seem to stay away from you."

SHE CAUSED HER OWN PROBLEMS AND THEN WOULD RATHER RISK INJURY/DEATH THAN FACE THE HUMILIATION. ARE YOU KIDDING ME?

This is more 4.5 stars because I loved it. It's one of my "I almost missed my subway stop" books. I met Sarah at BEA and was very excited to read her novel. I actually won a copy through Paper Lantern Lit. 
 Jenna lives in a small town, and all she wants to do is get out. But then she meets Ian and Luke, and things get more complicated than she ever imagined. 
 Love triangles have never been my favorite thing (I actually really hate love triangles), but if you are like me, you need to give Reclaimed a chance because it's not at all a traditional love triangle. I don't want to reveal too much because it will ruin everything, but I thought the whole concept was very well done and one I've not seen before. 
 I thought all of the characters were very well done -- well written and fleshed out and each of the three narrators had a distinct voice. You would probably be able to tell which one was narrating each section without the name informing you anyway. 
 As someone from a small town, the lives of the townspeople and the way they interacted was extremely believable. 
 Also, Sarah's prose was absolutely amazing. If I went through and highlighted my favorite lines, a good portion of the book would be yellow. 
 I HIGHLY recommend Reclaimed and will be eagerly anticipating Sarah's next novel.

Frustrating, in a good way. 
 My third book of his, not counting a smattering of stories here and there over the years. My bias going in to this: I did not enjoy Norwegian Wood but loved Hard-Boiled Wonderland (which I read first, having bought it used. The former was purchased by my younger self from the river before I knew a successful suicide.). 
 The first chapter of this is absolutely perfect in terms of construction. Murakami deftly weaves three disparate periods of time in the life of protagonist, Tazaki. By the end of the book, this middle ground is dropped and one character who is crucial to that part of the story disappears. Disappearance is a theme of this book, as is the shifting construction of identities. The irl group with which I read this book agreed that the middle timeline was the richest part of the text. One nested story within that may serve as a sort of key to deciphering the text as a whole, were one inclined to do so--this inner-story includes a dialogue on the worth of reason/intuition which reminded me very strongly of the Grand Inquisitor scene of the Brothers K. 
 Reading any book is a journey on the part of the reader; reading Murakami is all the moreso due to his keen sense of timing or kismet, which serves as a guide for the reader's personal development. At least that's how I feel in terms of reading-as-an-act-of-writing, or reading as a construction of meaning/experience.

On page sixteen, twelve-year-old Lakshmi asks her mother, "Why...must women suffer so?" Speaking from wisdom and resignation, Ama replies, "This has always been our fate...simply to endure...is to triumph." For the next 240 pages, Lakshmi endures more than western readers will want to imagine, and her triumphs are bitterly small. Her story is tragic and sad and distressingly common. For readers, McCormick's book is a challenge: just because things are so, must they remain that way? What can we do to make change? Can we do more than endure? What is triumph? 
 The story takes a while to ramp-up, and the first 40 pages will seem slow to readers who don't appreciate a slice of Nepalese mountain life. But the verse-style moves quickly once Lakshmi leaves her village, and it is hard to stop reading her story, as her voice becomes clearer. For a story about child sex-trafficking, "Sold" is honest without being explicit, making it a reasonable choice even for mature middle school audiences.

Wow! I'm still shocked about the end of this book; and possibly still a bit too overwhelmed to write a proper review, but i'll give it a shot: 
 Before i completely finished this book, I was ready to state that this one was the weakest book of the series so far. That it was still a damn good book in absolute, but somehow you just keep expecting utter brilliance from George RR Martin and anything less is a tiny dissapointment. Having just finished it, i have to add that the book ends a lot better than it begins. The last few hundred pages are definitely the best of the book, and let Martin's genious writing and storytelling show through again. 
 It's hard for me to pinpoint why exactly i liked this book less, (talking especially about the first 500pages now): 
 - Partly it has to do with the introduction of so many new characters we just don't care about. Or not yet at least. We never got to know them; he just throws his new leads into the story, immediately linked to half a dozen other new characters. That would have been fine had it been a few, but he introduces more than a dozen new lead characters, so it gets really hard. 
 - I also found the chapters more confusing in this book. Previously the chapter header immediately announces which part of the storyline is about to be told, so you can switch on the right parts in your brain so to speak. In this book very often he does not do that, and it takes you half a page or even a few pages before you know who is being featured in the chapter. I fully understand why he did that with Theon, Arya and young Griff - there it totally makes sense, but he did it very often where i didn't see the point. And it just made reading the book much more complex than it needed to me in my opinion. 
 - Something else that struck me in this book: one of the reasons i love Martin's books so much is that he doesn't work with good and bad. No-one is fully good nor fully bad; everyone is shades of grey somewhere between black and white. That makes these characters so real to me. Even the ones you like and would consider the good guys; they have clear flaws. And even though you might dislike other characters (Cersei!), you understand their reasons and they do show good sides, for the people they love for instance. 
 To me, Martin introduces in this book the first completely evil black character: the bastard of Bolton. Nothing, but really nothing, good about him. His father is slightly better, which makes the relationship between them so utterly unbelievable to me. But the introduction of this first fully evil character, that bothered me a bit. 
 The first few chapters went slow. I don't care much for Daenerys and she does not seem to do much but sit there somewhere in her city trying to solve a ton of issues that are not hers. But especially: who locks up a dragon?!? (insert angry face here) 
 The book clearly took off for me about half way through. I was full of excitement again when Brienne was back in the story. (BRIENNE! I love Brienne! I mean: Love love love her. And now that she is looking even uglier than before, I am really rooting for beauty and the beast type of storyline for her. She deserves it. I don't need (or want) a fully spelled out romance, but i do want the suggestion of a happy ending there. I hope Martin will give us (and them) that at least!) 
 Overall, despite the above comments, this is still a fabulous book. A little slower paced that i usually prefer, but nonetheless worth every minute i spent reading it. Rating-wise that would take me to a 4.5, but i graded it down because of the first 500 pages :) 
 Some final thoughts: 
 I can't shake this feeling that Arya (one of my other favs) is going to have such a critical role at the end of this story. I'm known to be wrong though i thought that about Jon too, especially since maybe, just maybe, he might have had Targaryen blood. But boy, despite all the warnings the red lady saw, i was shocked about what happened to him at the end of the book. . Arya my dear, you go girl! 
 I also like what he has done with Bran. I'm not entirely sure how that will contribute to the story. I can see that being very valuable to tell parts of the story, but i hope it will be more than that and that Bran will really contribute, and intervene somehow. He has already done that a little with Theon I suppose, but I'm expecting more! 
 Lastely, I love the way the Dothraki and the Unsullied speak. Sorry, let me rephrase that. This one loves the way they speak. This one really does. And now this one will go to bed.

First review of 2014...wohoo! 
 I like to think that I have eclectic reading tastes, meaning that while I have preferences when it comes to my reading choices, I find I like lots of different styles, genres, and stories for lots of different reasons. 
 But this ... The Cove, this is the kind of book that hits my literary G-spot. Okay, I know: a little crude, too much information, whatever--but true. 
 You see, I love Southern Gothic fiction--Flannery O'Connor, one of my heroines; Erskine Caldwell, a genius--so it's no surprise that I would enjoy Ron Rash's work. 
 And I did. I loved it. What's not to love? Subdued story and action; poetic prose; vivid descriptions; complex, flawed characters; and a tragic ending the reader hates to love and loves to hate.It's Southern Gothic fiction ... so you know it's coming. Still, you keep thinking maybe he won't do it. Maybe he'll let them live happily-ever-after. Please, let them live happily-ever-after. But he can't and you know it and I think that's part of the attraction of this genre.  
 And if that weren't enough, it's under 300 pages (the perfect length for a book as far as I'm concerned.) 
 This is the story of two siblings, misfits of a sort as far as the rest of their world is concerned, as they attempt to find some happiness, told against the backdrop of World War I and the South. 
 Bottom line: 5 sparkly, glittery, lovely little stars. I was lucky enough to check this out from the library the day before a big storm snowed us in. Definitely icing (or at least ice) on the cake. 
 Would recommend this to fans of Southern Gothic fiction.

 I fully support a character's sexuality being a casual part of their lives and not treated as some This Is A Very Special Episode Of type of way. I would love for there to be more of that both in books and on the screen. However, we already learn very quickly that Kyle is bisexual, he already knows and accepts this which is awesome, his best friend knows, and in almost a blink of an eye he comes out to his girlfriend and that's it. Or, until then Ruby decides to be upset about him not telling her sooner in the next chapter and they argue over it, but in another blink of an eye they're okay. Blink, Gideon realizes he's gay, blink, he's gay and in love with his best friend, blink, they open up about their feelings and kiss, blink, Kyle breaks up with Ruby and is almost smirking when he tells Gideon about it (ouch), blink, Gideon's family knows about their son and oh btw he's dating his bff and they're happy for him and end chapter.  
 Everything all happens so quickly, and so cleanly, that it was more like fanfiction written about middle graders. The only true tension lied with Kyle's learning disability, and Gideon's silly list, but again they barely turned into a full plot. Not to mention it is difficult to root for the love interests when I felt no chemistry between them. I didn't get a sense of how these two fell in love, what makes them so great together, nothing was earned. 
 It could have been a very cute and entertaining, fluffy story, but the execution fell flat. Then, of course I also have to accept that this isn't geared towards my age group. Also I am just never going to be a fan of author pandering pandering to fangirls and fanboys (references to LoTR, Parks and Rec, Chris Evans... Larry shippers? Aye)

 In London (1843) a pact is made between 4 wallflowers. They will help each other find husbands starting with the oldest and working down to the youngest. 
 (1) Annabelle is the oldest of the pact. Married - first book. 
 (2) Lillian is a rich American who has not acclimated to England. 
 (3) Evie is painfully shy and stutters. 
 (4) Daisy is the younger sister to Lillian. 
 Evie is in a predicament where her relatives are going to marry her off to her cousin so when her father dies his wealth will stay within the family. She's not fond of her relatives because they are mean to her and have kept her from being with her dying father. 
 Impulsively, Evie asks the rake Viscount St. Vincent (Sebastian) to marry her to avoid being married to her cousin. To her delight, he agrees to this marriage of convenience. Because of the situation, Evie is not concerned about his faithfulness. But like any good rake on his way to being reformed he wants to prove he can be a one-woman-man. Strangely enough, the parts of the book about the Fair were a lot more interesting and exciting to me than the parts about H.H. Holmes. Even though I bought the book expecting a murder story with the visits to the fair as backdrop, I think what I got was more about the construction of the fair with a few cons and killings over in the back corner. I don't want to make that sound like a bad thing though, because I honestly had fun reading this book. I really knew nothing about the Chicago World's Fair before I started reading this, and it was very exciting to see how many things appeared there for the first time ever, how many obstacles they surmounted and records they broke. 
 Even as someone who has a shelf here just for serial killers, Holmes was often a boring part of this story for me. Certainly more could have been done to make the Holmes storyline more exciting, but this is nonfiction and perhaps the source material no longer exists to support that. Although it came as a surprise to me, in my opinion the Fair is the main character, and I think it should be.

How do you review a literary classic? Once again I'm only reviewing as a plain reader point of view. I really liked this book. That's why I gave it four stars. Didn't give if 5 stars only because the first epoch gave me a hard time.

 I only had a hard time with the first part. Walter was way too poetic and rambled too much for my taste. Don't mean to be a feminist, but when it got to Marian's part of the story, that's where I got hooked. I want to read the first epoch again, now that I know Walter more, maybe if I re-read it I can see what I couldn't see about him the first time around. 
 I imagine the readers when this was first published as a newspaper serial, they must've been thrilled and dying to read the next part. That's how I felt after getting through with the first epoch. 
 The plot was very good. Not getting into details so I won't spoil your fun. It had all the twists and turns to make this a very enjoyable read. I liked that when I thought everything would or could be solved, there came a new twist. Just remember this was written in an era were there was no CSI or advanced forensic gadgets. Some twists and turns are guessable but despite of that they are enjoyable. 
 As for the characters, they play their part like they should. I hated Percival right from were he appears. Fosco gave me the creeps. I still picture him in my head and ewww he can't deny his two faced creepy personality. I wanted to slap Uncle Fairlie, he got on my nerves. Laura was your naive 1800's damsel in distress, Walter was OK (I like my men more manly than poetic he he) and Marian was the wonderwoman ahead of her time.  The Woman in White appears right from the beginning and the mystery behind her captures you right away. I would've liked it more if she had more appearances than the ones she had in the story. 
 If you're into long reads, filled with mistery, drama, treason, tragedy, love, sacrifice and friendship, then The Woman in White is for you.

So... Anna and the French Kiss, huh? I keep going between two and three stars, but my overly romantic brain has landed on three - for now. 
 The story is about Anna, who is forced to take her senior year in Paris, where she meets and falls in love with the beautiful and perfect St. Clair. 
 Quest: Get St. Clair. 
 Obstacle: He has a girlfriend. 
 You can figure out the rest of the story for yourself. 
 Yes, it is predictable. Yes, the protagonist is overly sensitive, dramatic and aggressive, yet so loved, while the love interest is overly beautiful, protective and humble, speaks British and French, and all the girls are in luuuv with him. Yes, it's totally cliche. 
 But somehow, despite the very weak characters and story, and waaay too many incredibly cheesy and bad lines, this book never bored me. Perkins has a light and funny way with words, and she is good with setting and day-to-day life. I'm a hopeless romantic, and I was charmed off my feet by a great part of Anna and St. Clair's relationship, even though Anna's behaviour was terribly frustrating sometimes. 
 Have you ever noticed how bad many authors, including women, are at writing young, female protagonists? Anna cries ALL THE TIME, she blames everyone else for everything and acts like a jealous girlfriend way before she and St. Clair even mentions their feelings. Yet he loves her sooo much, and she has lots of good friendships. She made me really tired after a while, as did St. Clair and their inability to communicate. Be very careful about publishing your NaNoWriMo novels, kids. 
 And if your most important question is if the boy is hot enough, chances are you're not writing a love story, despite what you think. 
 EDIT: Look, potential readers... If you love romance, this book is for you. Even if you'd prefer a real plot, it's very good at romance, and chances are you'll like it anyway. If you're not the kind who gets sentimental and giddy by teenage romance, if you're looking for something original that is not high school drama, then WALK AWAY. Right now. Anna and the French Kiss should have been a high school film, not a book. It's a typical high school film, which is fine, but if you're not into that, I'm positive you won't enjoy this book much. It's cute and funny and high school-y, and that works for some, but not everyone. Keep this in mind, both before you decide if you're going to read it, and (if you did read it even though you are not a high school drama kind of person) before you write an angry review. You might not be in the target audience.

In 1944, a seventeen-years-old American girl living with her relatives in London named Betty becomes Adele Blanchard and parachutes into Nazi-held France. Part of the British operation helping the French Resistance, she is to become a courrier in Paris while her friend Denise is to become a radio operator. They are first taken in by a welcoming French woman and her less-welcoming son, Pierre. For reasons unknown to Adele, she feels the need to prove herself to Pierre and volunteers to spy on a nearby factory. Denise and Adele head to Paris, rescuing a downed American pilot named Robbie along the way. He and Adele bond but they get separated upon reaching Paris. Their safe house compromised, they scramble to find safe places to stay. Once these are secured, the girls get to work helping the Resistance while Robbie waits to be returned to his unit. 
 First person present tense must be a growing fad in historical fiction. Once again, my usual complaints per my personal preference remain. But this one has an added reason--the story starts with Adele being tortured by the Germans. So most of the story is technically in flashback, so it should be in past tense. Which would also help when we find out more about Adele's life as Betty. I know many rules aren't set in stone, but I wish changing tenses was one. 
 Adele is a protagonist one can support, even if she wasn't our narrator. McAuley creates a portrayal of a young woman pretending to be older in a world that's all turned upside down. And she's trying not to die. I like how she's not immediately good at her job. She screws up her first drop. And she loses two bicycles. But she gets better and still manages to spy on the factory. She grows as an agent as D-Day approaches and develops a deep friendship with Denise as well as a relationship with Robbie. Along the way, she also manages to impress Pierre and he starts relying on her more. It makes you wonder how she ends up captured, but the reason is quite good and realistic. 
 The other characters are interesting as well. Denise at some times was annoying. You wanted to take her, shake her and remind her: "This is war, damnit!" She seemed more interested in being in Paris, shopping and partying. But when she flips out on a German soldier at a nightclub, a new side emerges. We learn her fiance died fighting the war and she's determined to bring down the Nazis. As the danger grows more imminent, she's a good soldier even when the enemy tricks her. In a twist that probably did happen, she uses different ways to tell the SOE she's operating under duress but the SOE never picks up on it. They even remind her of the sercurity protocols rather than panic over the fact she didn't perform them. Denise is also a driving force at the end to save Adele, rounding up people who are trustworthy.  She and Adele have a true friendship which is one of the best relationships in the book. 
 I do not think I will ever be adding this to my "romance" shelf. It doesn't fit in with the definition of "romance" held by the RWA and the industry. Neither her relationship with Robbie nor hers with Pierre is central to the book. Neither has a happily ever after or even happily for now. Pierre is killed by Germans. Robbie is revealed to still be France and he visits Adele when she is busted from a German prison. But he still has to continue to fight and only promises to find Adele once the war is over.  We do not see the end of the war so are not told if Robbie and Adele reunite. I personally would like to believe they do. Pierre was a distraction during the war. Two people facing possible death who found comfort in each other. Even Adele admits she prefers Robbie's company. And you can see the chemistry between them better. 
 McAuley creates a good picture of Paris under occupation. She also writes the tension the city was under well. 
 If it weren't for the present tense, I think this might have gotten 5 stars.

I assume most people have heard SOMETHING about this book by now. The impressions have been all over the place and impossible to avoid. So, if you want to remain totally impression free, don't continue reading, because I have not hidden the things I knew about the books before I read it. However, I don't feel like knowing what I did altered my reading experience. 
 When I first heard about this book, I wasn't sure if I wanted to read it. So when early reviews came out, I was not avoiding them like the plague. I saw enough to know that every blogger who mentioned this book was freaking out about some big twist. I was intrigued and decided to get in the hold line for this book at my library. However, it took two months for me to get a copy. Two months during which more people were reading it and clogging up all my blog and GR feeds with more impressions. The twist was never spoiled for me, I just knew that there was a twist and it was supposedly a doozy. 
 So I went into this book knowing that something big would happen and knowing full well that the title and blurbs mention lies. Lots of lies! Did I theorize before getting this book? Of course. Were any of those pre-theories correct? Far from it. My theories before seeing the book were more to do with identity. The narrator not being who she said she was - perhaps a bullied girl making up delusions that she was part of this distinguished family.  
 The truth of the book was much different than I had imagined from all the internet gossip. I did figure out the ending around halfway through, HOWEVER, I believe that even had I never heard of We Were Liars before I read it, the narrative itself was what led me to figuring it out. It's chock full of clues, that seemed (to me) to be pointing me boldly toward the truth. I don't think I figured this out simply because I was on high alert. I think that my reading background (I read mysteries, I like to theorize, I've read books with this EXACT same twist and knew some clues to look for) would have let me figure it out regardless of the hype. Did solving it early make the book any less enjoyable? Not at all. It was very fun to pick up on the small details. 
 The only disservice the hype did for me was make me feel like I was missing out on being mind blown. So many people were caught very off guard. I do remember the first time I read a twist like this I was totally blown away and went crazy over it. 
 So anyway, let's step away from discussing the twist and look at other elements of the story. 
 Things I loved: 
 -I read this book in about a day. It was short, engaging, and flowed well. It's not bogged down with filler. 
 -There is a map! And a family tree! 
 -Beach setting. 
 -Made up fairy tales. 
 -Mysterious happenings. 
 -Unreliable narrator. 
 What I didn't like: 
 -A lot of the dialogue and internal monologue seemed immature for the ages portrayed. At times it seemed more like I was reading about 12-13 year olds instead of 15-17 year olds. There are a couple of ways you can justify this in Cadence and her peers, but even the adult characters seemed immature to me. I am not familiar with the author's other work, but this read a bit more like middle grade fiction to me, which broke with the overall darker feeling I was getting from the plot. 
 If you care to read about how I broke down the mystery, keep reading. 
  
 -From page 5 we know that Cadence is an unreliable narrator because when she tells us her father left, she claims he then shot her in the chest and she bleeds to death on her front lawn. Then she just gets up and continues about her day normally. I know right away that I can't trust what she tells me. 
 -On page 32 we learn that she'd been in some sort of accident where she hit her head and almost drowned. Now she has migraines and selective memory loss. At this point my running theory is that Cadence is a ghost and doesn't know she is dead. She skips a summer at the island, and only talks to her mom and dad, is self admittedly invisible at school, and no one replies to her emails. Because I think she is a ghost at this point, I am watching for any clues that she interacts with characters besides her parents. Once she returns to the island for Summer 17, she does have many interactions, so I no longer think she is the ghost, but because I was on alert looking for interactions, I began to notice how The Liars never talked to anyone but Cady that summer. 
 -The Liars do not greet Cady (aside from waving) when she arrives at the island. 
 -The little cousins believe the Cuddledown house (Mirren's old house) is haunted, and Mirren's family has moved out of it. Everyone avoids it except for Cady and the Liars. 
 -The Liars never go to the nightly family dinners. No one cares that they aren't there. 
 -Other characters don't want to talk about any of The Liars when Cady mentions them. They change the subject almost imperceptibly. 
 -The Liars never interact with any character other than Cady during Summer 17. They are only shown with other characters during flashbacks to Summer 15, which were very cleverly placed. 
 -Cady spends a lot of time with The Liars on the tiny beach. Her mom knows she goes there, but thinks she is alone. 
 -Cady often says that she doesn't notice when The Liars approach or leave a room. 
 -Cady is admittedly high on Percocet the entire summer and is having hallucinations of people who aren't there. (A witch, who clubs her in the head with a statue, a man who hacks at her head with an axe, etc.) 
 -The scene that really solidified my theory was when Cady goes cliff jumping with The Liars (page 140). The boys jump, but then everyone insists it's too dangerous for Cady to do it too. Hmmm, could it be because they are already dead and can't be hurt?? 
 So when it was revealed that The Liars had died in the fire, I was not caught off guard or shocked. But I was excited to see all the clues pay off!

How have I missed this much lauded female sci-fi author until now?? I totally loved this book. It was suspenseful and well written and the perfect combination of scifi and historical fiction. That seems like a strange combination, since usually the genres are so different, especially in tone. But Willis blended them perfectly. However, mostly it read like historical fiction, so if you don't like historical fiction and think it's too slow (the most common complaint), then you probably won't like this book. But man was it well written. Willis really did her research. The characters were complex and interesting, and the depictions of medieval life were fascinating, though the scenes during the Black Plague were quite intense. After finishing the book, I found myself unconsciously being careful not to get too close to other people as if they might infect me! That's how powerful Willis' writing was. And though it was written in the 90s, the theme of plague/virus felt very pertinent to today given the recent H1N1 and TB scares. 
 Can't wait to read the next book in the series.

 The first quarter of the book, I struggled to get into the story. 
 Georgia, is perfectly good, too perfect in fact, one who doesn't own any mean bone in her body. She is a small town country girl who loves horses and whose loving parents fosters messed up kids. And just like the people around her small town, she is curious about Moses, the little baby that was left in a basket at a dingy Laundromat, born to a crack addict. The troublemaker, delinquent crack baby who became her hero. And she plans to court Moses until he is hers. 
 To begin with, I just find Georgia obsessed with Moses! A young sweet girl who has a huge crush. And the more Moses turns her away, the more she chases after him. She definitely cannot get enough about Moses's eyes! 
 .. 
 his oddly-colored eyes... 
 his light eyes... 
 his yellowish-green animal eyes... 
 those weird wolf eyes... 
 his cool eyes... 
 his golden-green eyes.. 
 I did wish Georgia shows just a little bit more attitude along the way... to be angry and have some fight. 
 Moses, is a troubled guy who is fighting some inner battles. He is a loner who is obsessed with painting. He lives by his own law... 
 "Thou shall paint. Thou shall leave and never look back. Thou shall not love." 
 I thought Moses was plain Trouble with a capital "T" that seriously needs help at the start of the story. But then again, there were some unexplainable things he does that lead me to thinking there was definitely more to Moses than meets the eyes. Here enters the paranormal side of the story. (To avoid spoiler, I will leave it to you to find out what it is about.)

 That said... halfway through the book, I was hooked! I was intrigued by the mystery that surrounds the story, as it progresses on a slightly higher level of emotional struggle. 
 I couldn't help but wonder though.... There is a time lapse here as the story moves forward seven years later, as a lot has happened inside that same time frame. Seven years seems a long time and I wondered, if not for Eli, would Moses come back to Georgia?  
 I loved the twists and surprises and I did like the the second chance romance ... and that perfect ending. 
 Now I'm curious about Tag, Moses's best friend.... ;)

******CRIME FIGHTERS!****** 
 Suspense, Paranormal and Romance 
 Marlie's a psychic who after a six years of having no psychic episodes is now seeing horrific murders through the eyes of the murderer. After the first episode she contacts the Orlando police department with the goal of helping them but knowing she'll be their number one suspect since she can describe in detail the whole murder scene. Marlie is empathetic; she sees and feels the emotions of other people. 
 Dane's an Orlando police detective who isn't buying Marlie's story that she is a psychic. He believes she is involved somehow in these murders. He finally realizes to solve this crime spree he needs to work with Marlie. 
 The Murderer is meticulous in the details of the hunt. He studies his prey and learns their lifestyle. Mostly women are his prey but there are a few men who meet his criteria for needing to be taught a lesson. He has rules he follows to insure he won't be caught and at the same time he still gets to enjoy the power he wields over his victims. These aren't random murders ...these are well thought out murders to right the world of rude people. 
 I'm not a fan of instant of love but I'm going to give this a pass because I really enjoyed the story. It had me on my edge of my seat at the end of the book. 
 Standalone

Garrett Graham may have ruined me for all other book boyfriends--which is disappointing, because I have a good list going. 
 He may have been frustrating at times, but I loved the heck out of him. He was so patient and considerate when it came to helping Hannah with her "problem," yet the corresponding scenes were treated with the appropriate amount of awkwardness and hesitancy. While those of Garrett's peers who idolize him do so because he's a hockey jock, there is much more to him than his athletic prowess. And, as readers discover through Hannah, there's more to him than his sexual prowess as well. 
 In addition to loving Garrett, I really liked the heroine. She didn't make any incredibly stupid decisions (like we see happen frequently with MCs in NA), and I found her to be level-headed, intelligent, and genuine. 
 The characterization in this book is on point: from the dialog to the action to the inner monologue, I found myself knowing and loving the characters--and not just the MCs. There's a great cast of secondary characters present here, and I look forward to hearing their stories in subsequent "Off-Campus" installments. 
 Now, I can't in good faith finish this review without mentioning two of my favorite parts, the "campus-wide hands-off law" and the "penis convention" (locker room scene) . It's kinda ridiculous how much I laughed at not only these concepts, but the rest of the novel as well. 
 Puck bunnies--the term, not the concept--was a new one for me. 
 I'm experiencing a serious book hangover after this one! I even googled "books like The Deal" so that I could follow the novel with something similar in content and caliber, but I haven't yet come up with any viable options. 
 Sure, there are a lot of elements here that we've seen in NA before, but there were enough twists and fresh material to keep this from teetering into cliche territory. 
 I know we're only in the third month of 2015, but this definitely ranks among my favorites from this year. I highly recommend it as a sweet, swoon-worthy, low-angst read for fans of new adult and romance.

 Tash Hearts Tolstoy was a perfectly lovely, diverse read with epic friendships and awesome parents (!) that I probably should have loved a lot but instead... I'm kind of swaying on that thin border between love and like and hoping I don't fall to my death on someone's torch or pitchfork. Because yes, this book had lots of awesome things that I loved but it also had things I had issues with and that make me wail in agony because I wanted to adore this book. But I just kind of loved it. Which makes me sad. 
 I really want to start out with saying that I really enjoyed the writing and it was super easy for me to get into. I have had the author's other book Lucky Few on my TBR for a while now but have never gotten to it, which I should probably fix asap. Especially now that I've read this book because her writing is really my style and I've heard good things about it so what am I waiting for really? For my TBR to shrink down to a reasonable and managable size? Because that's never going to happen ever. Nobody should expect their TBR to do that because it's a hopeless cause. This review is the perfect example because I'm giving you another book to put on yours. You're welcome. 
 Another win in this book is the diversity because there's a lot of it! Tash is asexual, which is AMAZING, because I need more ace rep in YA. Being of the ace spectrum myself. But there's also a teeny tiny gay romance in the background which I honestly would like to read about more?? Maybe we can have this book from their perspective? YES PLEASE. Also I'm 99% sure Tash is biracial too. And her dad is a chef. This doesn't really relate to diversity except for the diverse foods that are eaten in this book, which, let's be honest, is very important diversity as well. Food is important, people. It's nice to see people in books actually eat. 
 We also have a very accurate rep of the effort it costs to maintain a blog/youtube channel and handle the social media, especially the trolls. Because it's a LOT of work and there's a lot of mean people out there in the interwebz. I'm lucky enough to not be famous and popular (*cries*) so I really haven't experienced that side of things myself but I know others who have and I see it a lot. It was nice to see that it wasn't all rainbows and sunshine for Tash and Jack. 
 Speaking off, I loved the friendships in this book a lot. I am a big fan of positive friendships in YA and think books need that more. Like a lot more. Jack and Paul are siblings and Tash's best friends and they were the best. I loved Jack, who is not very good at the emotional stuff but that kind of made her adorable in my eyes? I know, weird. Paul is the most precious of everyone and I just wanted to cuddle him. Also awesome parents. YAY. Yes please! I loved Tash's parents. Her father is a chef. I mean... Obviously I love him. 
 BUT HERE IS WHERE THE TROUBLE STARTS. Because while I did love Jack and Paul and their sibling bond is the best thing ever... I didn't really love Tash herself? Like... I liked her and stuff, but she was so frustrating sometimes and I didn't really think she changed all that much? Also I spent like 80% of this book pronouncing her name wrong in my head. It wasn't until she explained how to do it to another character that I found out myself. WHAT IS THIS. MY LIFE IS A LIE. I also kindly want to stab Thom with a rusty spork for the comments he made when Tash told him about her asexuality. Like no. No dude. Just stop. Go fling yourself through the window. Please and thank you.  
 Also the cast of the web-series was not THAT big but I did get confused sometimes keeping them all apart? But I didn't have trouble with the two guys that end up being an item because of course I wouldn't get confused by those two. I still vote for this book to be rewritten from their perspective and also released like next month or something. That'd be lovely. 
 Aaaand unfortunately I wasn't into the romance the whole time. It was kiiind of a love-triangle that I didn't like and found frustrating until the third person was out and it was just the main ship and they got their act together. So I liked the romance at the end. But up until then it was just... nope for me. And sometimes things got a bit too dramatic and I don't like unnecessary drama, people. You know this. 
 And lastly, I didn't really see the point of Klaudie?? Like... yay for sisters and siblings and all but what was the point of her? WHY did she suddenly act all stupid? Just to add more drama to the story because if that's the case... Again, unnecessary drama + me = no. So yeah. I didn't really see the point of her being there. Sorry? 
 Overall I did really enjoy this book a lot. I even mildly and cautiously loved it. But I had issues with it that stopped me from really loving like I wanted to. I still thing you should read this if you're a fan of YA Contemporary AND especially if you're a youtuber/vlogger and very active on social media and the likes. Because this might just be super relatable to you. And also yay ace rep because we need more of this! So go read this book at your earliest convenience.

Though this is a "stand alone" novel, I am glad I have read both Fangirl by Rainbow Rowell and Harry Potter by J. K. Rowling because otherwise I may have been a bit lost. The plot is that it is the final year at a magical boarding school and Simon Snow is The Chosen One-- the one who will put an end to the Insidious Humdrum, the evil that is eating away the magic of the magic world. Simon has an intelligent side-kick, Penny, a graceful girlfriend, Agatha, and an archrival for a roommate, Baz (who is also a vampire and currently missing at the start of the book and driving Simon crazy about it). The Mage is the headmaster of the magic school and is also the leader of the magic world. He acts as a mentor towards Simon. 
 It plays so much off Harry Potter that I don't think it stands quite on its own. I feel like the reader needs prior exposure to a school of magic with a chosen one to really understand what is going on. On top of that, the actual plot is just too cliche. The Insidious Humdrum is actually caused by Simon's existence. This is due to his father, The Mage (who he doesn't know is his father) being obsessed with a prophecy of a mage who will come to the magic world at its greatest time of need so he impregnated his wife and performed spells to create that person. His wife dies in labor and he sends Simon off to the normal world to be raised hidden away until the prophesied time comes when he needs him. Also there is a side-plot of Simon receiving a message from Baz's mother's ghost to tell Baz about her death which is actually a murder and who knows the details. Basically the Mage is also the cause of Baz's mother's death, too.  If this was the 8th and last book of a well loved fantasy series and that was the plot outcome I would be so displeased as a reader! The plot stands just fine on the fact that it is a standalone, which it is, but at the same time its supposed to represent something more than that, which it doesn't. 
 Despite that, I still really liked the book. I was just adsorbed by the characters. I think Baz has the best introduction of any character ever. I love how he pokes fun at Simon. I like how Penny is Ron and Hermoine wrapped in one character so she's smart and a great friend who doesn't mind breaking the rules and her loyalty means everything. Simon's all right and I like Agatha's ending She just didn't belong in the magical world. And the fact that she thinks Lucy got away just sorta proves her naivety of it all.  We get a really interesting way of telling a backstory Through Lucy's point of view . I like how magic spells can be catch phrases that can also lose power over time as people stop using them (think of the memes and the power they could have!) It was a quick read and I was giving it 4 stars until I got to the plot resolution where it was falling quickly to three, but the overall readability of it was still very good and I really like the alternating points of view to give the story a good pace. I really liked reading it but I only liked/tolerated the actual plot. I'll give it 4 stars.

I loved all of the characters more than ever. There were so many impactful scenes and shocks and great line delivery. I thought things played out how they needed to in this world. I really thought she'd have more of a moral dilemma but instead she's just running around shooting first and asking questions later. I don't read a lot of non-fiction, but when I do I go for, as I call them, Funny Lady Memoirs. Tina Fey, Amy Poehler, Mindy Kaling, Amy Schumer. While there were definitely things I enjoyed from each of their books, Lauren Graham's Talking as Fast as I Can: From Gilmore Girls to Gilmore Girls, and Everything in Between is by far my favorite. I have loved Lauren Graham as a long time fan of Gilmore Girls and reading this book just made me love her even more. I loved that while there was a lot more to the book than Gilmore Girls and Parenthood, there were dedicated sections to each show and even though I didn't get any great inside scoop, I was able to tell how much these shows mean to her and that she's happy to be connected with them. 
 Some fun things I learned: 
 -Lauren Graham was attached to another show when she was cast in Gilmore Girls and if that show had been renewed for a second season she never would have been Lorelai Gilmore. 
 -Lauren and Alexis Bledel (Rory) didn't meet until after they were both cast in the show. 
 -While Gilmore Girls is famous for it's super long scripts (due to how fast they talk!), Parenthood's dialogue wasn't as strict and allowed for a lot more "collaboration." Which I think proves my theory that instead of lines, the script just directs them to "Stutter and Cry." 
 -Lauren and her Parenthood daughter Mae Whitman are producing partners and sold an adaption of The Royal We (one of my favorite reads of 2016), which Lauren is writing. **I tried to find info for this on IMDB, but couldn't, so I'm not sure what the status is, but I'm very excited for this!** She is also writing a second novel, but not a lot of details on that yet. 
 -**Mild spoiler for the Gilmore Girls reboot** When Lauren found out the Final Four Words, she didn't think it was an ending, but a cliffhanger. Every time she mentions that to the creator of the show, Amy Sherman-Palladino just smiles. So maybe more Gilmore Girls to come? 
 Overall 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Talking as Fast as I Can. I liked that Graham didn't seem to take herself too seriously and the whole book had such a fun feeling to it. Okay, so I'll admit that part of the reason I wanted to read this book was to see if it really was written in the style of an internet puppy. For those baffled by that comment, see Priestgate 2012. However, that's not the only appeal of the book. It's a detective story set in the very near future, with minimal but incredibly interesting science fiction elements. It's also not set in the USA or London, which makes a nice change. The story takes place mainly in Edinburgh, and the culture, the people, the language, etc, were all quite familiar to me, bringing back happy memories from four years at university in Scotland (I was 1 hour from Edinburgh by train). So, lots that grabbed my interest. 
 The story of Rule 34 is quite unique. Rule 34 refers to an internet rule: if it exists, there is porn of it. In the book, the Rule 34 squad is a police force that watches porn sites looking for evidence of criminal activity, on the theory that all crimes will become fetishised eventually on the internet. Liz, one of the three main characters of the book, is a detective who has been demoted from Homicide to managing the Rule 34 squad. However, when Liz becomes involved with investigating a murder that has sexual overtones, and when this turns into a string of murders and then into a full-on potential serial-killer situation, she is drafted in to help with the case. 
 I was really in two minds about this book. On the one hand, it has a great concept and one of the best serial-killer identities I've come across, and the mystery was impressively complex and involved. There's the Rule 34 squad, Liz's stalled career and love life, murders, a break-away Eastern European republic, connections to Artificial Intelligence, and many more subplots, which are all expertly woven together. The book is very clever, and perhaps a little too clever, as there was quite a bit that still left me baffled at the end. I did really enjoy the ending and thought it was appropriate for the story, but by that point ATHENA's motivations completely confused me . I also felt that the book may have been over-long, and it took a very long time for me to actually get into it. Once I finally did feel grabbed by the story, I was absolutely hooked and found it compelling reading, but for me it had a shaky start. 
 I also hated the second person point of view. This switches between three main characters, and just as I would be drawn into the story enough to ignore it, the point of view would switch and I would be jolted back into noticing the second person again. The ending at least provided some context for the use of second person, with a very interesting suggestion as to whose point of view we might actually have been seeing events through all along. But then, Charles Stross has used second person before, so it might just be his thing. Even if used for a good narrative reason, I still found it irritating and distracting. 
 However, there was a lot that I loved about the novel. I thought Charles Stross did a brilliant job of capturing Edinburgh and Scottish society without resorting to silly cliches, and I also thought his characters were fantastic. They all came to life, and felt like completely different people. No-one spoke with the same voice as anyone else, despite the confusion of the second person style. There was a lot of diversity in the characters offered - a lesbian police detective, a bisexual Scottish-Pakistani Muslim, a mentally ill man, and an Eastern European country trying to combat international crime. Charles Stross seems to have avoided obvious or tired stereotypes at every turn. The main characters in particular were amazing; Liz felt completely real - likeable and human - and Anwar was always sympathetic even when breaking the law or making bad choices. The Toymaker, the most conventional 'bad-guy' of the novel had depths to his character that were both fascinating and horrifying. Everyone, even if they only popped up for a chapter, was carefully written. 
 So, this one was perhaps a bit of a mixed bag. There was a lot to love and a lot that would make me recommend the book, but I would also have to advise readers to stick with it if the beginning seems like a bit of a slog. However, there was plenty about it that frustrated me too, and parts of it, in particular the more technical aspects, still have me confused. But, for its defiance of the usual stereotypes and tropes that come with the genre, and for its excellent characters and complex mystery, this book is worth a read.
