Scarlett, the older sister, who has tasked herself with protecting Tella at all costs, doesn't want to risk their father's wrath. He has set up a marriage for her to take place during Caraval. She sees it as her only way to escape her father's island. She plans on taking Tella with her when she gets married. Of course Tella knows that Scarlett will never go willingly to Caraval, so she makes plans of her own. She enlists the help of a young sailor, Julian. They arrive just in time to participate in this year's Caraval performance. Only this year's performance is different. It revolves around Scarlett and Tella. Legend, the master of Caraval, kidnaps Tella and the object of this year's game is to find her. Whoever finds her first wins a wish. The rules of the game are simple: Everything that happens at Caraval is part of the performance, it isn't real. Players are warned to not get too swept up in the game. The problem is, Scarlett can't help but wonder if this year is different. This year it's personal and she is determined to save Tella before it is too late. Scarlett is forced to push herself beyond her breaking point and truly learn who she is and what is truly important to her. She is forced to look inside herself and overcome her fears. This is a very fun adventure where the twists and turns keep you on the edge of your seat. What is real and what is just part of the game? Who can be trusted? I really enjoyed the characters and getting to know them through all the trials and tribulations they had to embark on. This was a very fun story that kept me guessing the entire way through. The ending sets up the next adventure quite nicely. I am definitely excited to see what comes next. I would love to get to know the mysterious Legend a little bit more.

This book isn't quite what I expected. While I avoided spoilers, I read lots of reviews that talked about how Dangerous Girls totally screws with your head (in more colorful language) and for the most part I didn't feel like that when I was reading it. But once I finished it, yeah, I think I agree. 
 Anna, Elise and their friends appear to be the typical YA party girls. They are rich and spoiled and completely unlikable. I definitely have to give props to Haas's writing when it comes to the character development. It's definitely hard to have main characters that are so unlikable, with little to no redeeming qualities, and still come out the other side with such an intense emotional payoff. 
 It's impossible not to mention the similarities to the Amanda Knox headlines. There are a lot of similarities between Anna and Amanda. Both are seen soon after the crime to be canoodling with their boyfriends. Both have an unusually calm reaction to the murder of their friend. Both are villainized in the public eye with little to no real evidence supporting their guilt. I followed a lot of the Knox trial so I found the similarities in the crime and ensuing investigation really interesting. 
 While the trial and the murder mystery is definitely a big part of the novel, the relationship between Anna and Elise is really the central part of the story. Their friendship is intense, co-dependent, toxic. There are lesbian undertones that have you continually second guessing through the story whether they're just affectionate teenage girls or something much more. It's almost hard to say whether Elise is more obsessed with Anna or if Anna is more obsessed with Elise. Again, Haas's writing is almost flawless in this regard. 
 I enjoyed the timeline jumping through the chapters. We skip around from the vacation, to when Anna and Elise first meet, to the trial, and more multiple times and it just works. Not all authors could pull this off so cohesively, but it's done really well here. There is a twist ending and while there were times that I almost guessed it was going to turn out that way, I wasn't expecting it by the time we actually got there. My only real problem with the ending is that I found it a bit confusing at first, as things are obviously suggested, but not specifically revealed. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Dangerous Girls. I found it to be a very compulsive read that I could hardly put down. I read it in two sittings and honestly considered calling in a vacation day at work today so I wouldn't have to go to bed last night (alas, my vacation leave did not support that idea). It was an intense, well-written, character-driven novel and I would recommend it to fans of crime, YA, Amanda Knox-like headlines and Gone Girl. I'm looking forward to reading Dangerous Boys!

I would give this brilliant masterwork by Dostoevsky more stars if I could. 
 This is the story of a man intensly divided in his mind, completely crushed by poverty and squalor, but possesses an intellectual caliber so lofty, it gives rise to pride and ego quite difficult to handle.  Set in the great city of St. Petersburg during pre-evolutionary 18th century Russia, and through an unusual combination of circumstances and ideals, Raskolnikov, our main protagonist, is incited to murder. 
 In a belief which when closely examined might not seem so addled, he comes to the conclusion that humanity is divided into two segments, those with the ability to bring utilitarian good, and those without it. He argues that there exists an echelon of Napoleon-like men, who are allowed to transgress laws because in doing so, they bring about a desirable result for all. Also, in the success of their initiatives, old rules are demolished and new ones are set, allowing them to transcend punishment. The same concept follows the idea of revolutionaries who, in succeeding to overthrow standing government, punish other revolutionaries who try to oust them, even though it is the same process once used to achieve their own goals. 
 Once the murder is committed, and perhaps even before so, Raskolnikov begins his journey of suffering, punishment, and for the least part, atonement. 
  
 I really don't know where to begin with the review of this novel. Every single aspect brought forth by Dostoevsky has a purpose and a meaning. The characters have such rich and colorful psychological profiles, the symbolic dreams of Raskolnikov and Svidrigailov, each dealing with issues brought on by their subconscious minds and leading them to action, the weak-mindedness of Katerina Ivanovna as she wastes away because of her intense suffering (not to mention consumption), the extreme smoothness of Porfiry Petrovich in his battle of wits with Raskolnikov, Marmeladov's story which sets the tone for the entire plot with a heartrending account of his family's troubles, brought on solely by himself. And Sonya, dear poor timid Sonya, forced to prostitute herself to support her family, consisting of her drunken, irresponsible and masochistic father (Marmeladov), her hysterical and delirious step-mother (Katerina Ivanovna), and her underfed, dirty step-siblings. 
 There are also all sorts of themes, motifs, and symbols in the book, the color yellow for instance, associated with dirtiness and poverty, and later on symbolizing guilt and insanity. The crossing of bridges, as if crossing over into a different realm of mentality for Raskolnikov. Crossroads, and their implication of a turning point. Going to America, being associated with a place for the guilty to escape. Alienation from society, the crudeness of the typical Russian peasant, the psychology of crime and punishment, how a criminal in reality longs to be caught and punished because deep inside, he harbors guilt. Dostoevsky's unconventional nihilism makes its way and shows itself tremendously in the character of Raskolnikov, his utter disregard for social order and the emotions of others, as well as his dialogue with other characters in the book. 
 This is the second book I've read for Dostoevsky, the first being The Brothers Karamazov and some people would insist on the superiority of the former to the latter, I've spent quite a bit of time considering this, and have decided that even though murder is a large part of both novels, such a comparison cannot be made. To start with, they are both of different genres, Crime and Punishment being a psychological drama, and The Brothers Karamazov being realist fiction, second the themes and motifs presented in each are completely different from each other, for Crime and Punishment it's the points I've mentioned above, while for Karamazov, it's the conflict of faith and doubt, moral responsibility and its possible roots in religion, as well as the burden of free will. The nature of the protagonists is completely different as well, Raskolnikov being a misanthrope, an outcast of society disliked by most people who chance to meet him, while Alyosha Karamazov is the closest embodiment of an angel on earth, pure in spirit and going about charming one person after another. They are simply different animals. 
 A great pleasure indeed. If you're going to read this book, and I beg you to do so, please read the unabridged translation by Richard Pevear and his wife Larissa Volokhonsky. I urge you to check out The Brothers Karamazov as well, it is also well-worth your time.

I'm a sucker for good robot books, and this is one of them. The story is told through various flashbacks from different points of view, kind of like World War Z. The actual premise used for gathering these points of view is very hokey, but I'm not sure I could have come up with anything better. The stories themselves are excellent, with different viewpoints and opinions on the same events, with many of the characters coming together by the end of the book. 
  
 The robots themselves were varied and wonderful, though some of the techniques used to employ them for human use seemed a little contrived. The "evil" robots that Archos evolved were truly frightening, between the beetle-like creatures that exploded when they detected body heat, or the pluggers that rooted around in the blood stream until they got to a person's heart then exploded. 
 There were a few problems though. The first was why Archos didn't just use nerve gas or some other agent to kill people, but I guess that can be covered with the "He was only trying to kill humans and wanted to save all other life on the planet" idea that is repeated a couple of times in the book. I also am not sure why Archos made chimeric androids, other than to give the character Mathilda power. I think there should have been a chapter or two with a mole android or a person used as a walking bomb after they'd infiltrated a human camp. There were allusions to this in the book, but no examples. Also, the good robot 902 seemed like a deus ex machina that was put in to help the author out of a jam as much as he helped the main characters out of a jam. I'd give 902 a rating of .6 Gandalf, where a full Gandalf is an all-powerful character that conveniently disappears and reappears to use their super-human power to help the mortal heroes out of a jam.

One of the themes of the book seems to be that a zombie's life isn't terribly different than the lives we lead now, going from work to home to work, grimly making the rounds of gym, school, what-have-you, but I guess I'm a hard sell on that.  Wow this novel was totally out of my element and pushed me so far past my comfort zone, the hero's were not hero's at all, I don't even believe they were anti-hero's, no they were just straight up badass villains. The things that they did were deplorable and yet I found myself rooting for them throughout the whole thing! The mafia in this novel live by a code and the one above them all is: family comes first, protect those in your circle... any one else can fucking burn in hell. Melody say's something in this novel that totally made sense in a really sick and twisted way: "I do care about God, and I do believe in Him. (I really did). However, I know why I was created. God needs me. What would happen if there weren't people like me? If the world were perfect, if everything was the way you wished it to be, then why would you pray? God needs me, because without us, you forget about Him. He is on my side, not yours." ... I know sick right but in a way I totally fucking get it and see where these people are coming from. 
 "He was known as the 'Boogeyman of the East'..." 
 Liam Callhan aka Caenn na Conairte was a complete monster... and I loved every minute of it (God what has this book turned me into?) I literally laughed when he would let other people feel his wrath, maybe it was because he was so calm about the whole thing, but holy crap that man is a maniac. I like that the author made his character's fault be that he is afraid of loneliness, and that he was the one pushing for a loving marriage with his wife, instead of the other way around because you so rarely see that nowadays. 
 "and I was unknown 'Wicked Witch of the West.'" 
 Melody Giovanni aka The Boss was one scary ass bitch. I totally loved her, she too had me cackling at all the destruction she caused but if I was ever in the same room as her I would literally roll up in a ball in some corner and play dead, like that's how scary she is. She was by far one of the strongest heroine's I have ever read about, she did not allow her past to overcome her, and she also refused to be affected by stereotypical gender classes. I love the moments when she allowed herself to actually feel for others, it was very touching. 
 The Caenn na Conairte and The Boss together? Were the most scariest people in the entire universe... 
 "Who was the biggest fuck up?" She asked softly. I noticed she never really yelled at the men when she was pissed off. In fact, her voice became softer, as though she wanted to haunt those around her. 
 No one spoke up, so I walked up beside her, leaning against the table. "She asked a question. We want an answer, or we will kill you all and start over. How much do we pay them, love?" 
 ... S C A R Y ! 
 However they were also beautiful and sweet ... when they weren't watching live footage in their marriage bed of people's home's being blown up... by them... 
 The writing was decent, minor typo issues and etc. but considering the fact that the author is twenty something and still in school, I mean come on what exactly have a lot of people accomplished by their early twenties? The story-line and the characters outweigh the issue of the writing. I would recommend this book to those people who enjoy dark romance because this definitely was dark, or also to those people who don't mind being pushed just a little past their comfort zone.

Death is not a fearful thing, it's living that's treacherous. 
 Jim Jones November 18, 1978 
 I was only seven when the massacre/mass suicide at Jonestown occurred, and while I always had a general sense of what happened, until reading this book, I lacked a true appreciation for the magnitude and bizarre nature of this tragedy. 
 From champion of the oppressed to drug-addled megalomaniac, Jim Jones was an enigma on many fronts. He started off speaking out against racism and segregation, and promoting equal rights in the context of an admirable socialist platform, but ended up a paranoid drunk/drug addict who organized the mass murder of over 900 of his followers, more than a third being children. 
 Scheeres wants her readers to understand not only why church members were attracted to Jones in the first place, but why they stayed. She realizes it's easy to marginalize his followers as cult members and all the negative associations/assumptions that go with that. After all, normal people don't join cults, right? People don't ever believe stupid, crazy things and, worse, act crazy and stupid based on those beliefs...ever. 
 In fact, she goes out of her way not to refer to Jones and his followers as a cult. 
 She offers a satisfactory retelling of the timeline of events and manages to bring a few of the characters to life through journal entries, recordings, and letters. She touches on the circumstances that brought various people into the church, whose greatest selling point seemed to be that it offered a community of acceptance particularly for African Americans (who accounted for about 70% of the church membership even as the majority of church leaders were white). 
 She explores the growth of the Jones' ministry, which motivated members with passionate diatribes about social injustices and dazzled them with festive sermons featuring awe-inspiring miracles (albeit ones he orchestrated behind the scenes.) She describes Jones as a religious zealot, charlatan, and megalomaniac, among other things, who used sex with both men and women, isolation, manipulation of food, drugs, and other various techniques to get them to sign over their money and ultimately their lives. She paints Jones as a crazed or rather crazy, self-proclaimed revolutionary with a death wish, not only for himself but for his entire congregation. 
 Her recounting succeeds on many levels, but fails on others. She seems determined to characterize Jim's followers as helpless victims, and on many fronts they were. But I'm not sure she offers anything new. She certainly doesn't explore the complex nature of "brain washing." In fact, I found this 2006 documentaryto cover what she did in the book but with the added bonus of hearing directly from former members who survived. 
 I also listened to that last suicide meeting, which was taped by Jones and later found and then released by the FBI. It's both chilling and sobering. 
 I've ordered two more books on the topic, one written by Tim Reiterman, a reporter who visited Jonestown the day before the massacre and who-- along with other press members, Senator Ryan, and several defectors-- was gunned down by members of the settlement (on Jones' orders no doubt) as they tried to leave. The other is written by a survivor and one of Jones' mistresses. 
 I'll be interested to see how this book stacks up.

I've read there are 80s publishing reasons for the first two Lioness books being whirlwinds, but this one slows things way down. And I like it better for it, as a grown-up reading now. I read another review that spoke to problems in the way Pierce wrote of the Bazhir, who (both in this book and the first one) are written as a ignorant and savage culture. In the Woman Who Rides Like a Man, Alanna infiltrates this culture and becomes something a savior (also related to events in the first book) that enables her to make more changes within this male-dominated foreign culture than she has (so far) actually made within her own. Jonathan also swoops in to become a hero/savior to them. Are these things problematic? Why yes, possibly; I think it's a very fair critique. 
 I like how Jonathan is revealed to be the whiny, paternalistic brat he truly is and that Alanna holds her own and never marries him. This is not something I really appreciated as an kid, and so was a great story for me to read at the time. As an adult, I can see how their relationship was problematic from the beginning as he, being older and more powerful and the Prince and also one of the only people who knew she was female, kind of took advantage of her. This one takes close concentration and effort. Mantel's writing here is so dense that you have to constantly pay attention to figure out who is speaking and being described. It not only defuses formerly-held beliefs you may have had about the reign of Henry VIII (Thomas More was not the sympathetic objector portrayed in "A Man for All Seasons" and he certainly was no saint), but it also presents an interesting portrait of a man who is somewhat in the shadows of history but was front and center at the time.

My boyfriend has a knack for knowing when I reach the last 20 pages of a book and chooses that moment to badger me with questions or otherwise distract me. (Even if he's not home at the time, it's uncanny, I'll start getting texts as soon as I near the finish line.) But as I dove into the final story in The Tsar of Love and Techno, he knew to leave me alone. I was barely keeping it together over on my end of the couch and he would have had to deal with unintelligible sobs if he so much as asked, "What do you want for dinner?" 
 So I guess you could say I had a strong emotional response to this book. Marra really knows how to wield that deadly combination of humor and sadness. He knows just how to make you lower your guard, and then before you know it he's punched you in the gut, you're uncontrollably weepy, and snot is running down your face. Not just any book can make me feel so vulnerable. 
 The Tsar of Love and Techno is a series of time-hopping short stories that each revolve, in some way, around the actions of a Soviet censor. Using multiple narratives, Marra shows us the many ways that art can hurt, heal, inspire, and betray us. He shows that there is beauty in the pain and absurdity of life, and that can sometimes be our only comfort. Each character has depth and complexity, each is meticulously and expertly rendered. Each story is good enough on its own that it could serve as a stand alone, but together they're something else.

I found this to be a solid 4 star read for me. My love for motorcycle romance started years ago after watching the tv show - SOA (which really isn't a romance tv series). I was drawn to the gritty world of bikers. So, when I discovered there were books that were about motorcycle clubs and they had romance in them, I knew I found a genre I'd be reading a lot of. 
 Emily is a 17 years old who has spent her life in the dark about her mother and biological father's past. She's met her father a few times but she's been indifferent towards him. He gave up his rights to her when she was little and so she's given up really caring who he is. 
 Emily's world is full of secrets she's not privy to. Everyone around her feels it's in her best interest to leave those secrets buried except for one person. That person can't divulge the secret but they become the guiding light in helping Emily uncover what has been kept from her all her life. 
 I try to avoid books that have cancer in them and when I found out one of the side characters had cancer I was already invested in the story. So, I made the decision to continue on. I appreciated that even though the character had cancer the reader didn't have to go through all the symptoms of cancer with that character. We never even find out what type of cancer the characters has because it wasn't about the tragedic effects of cancer but instead how it brought an estranged family together. 
 This is my first young adult mc romance. For those who like the atmosphere of the club life but want a tamer version of that environment, this is a good one try. 
 NOWHERE BUT HERE is a young adult motorcycle romance. It's set in the same universe as Walk the Edge , Long Way Home, and Untitled. Each one can be read as a standalone but the characters are interconnected.

Tana French's The Likeness closed right over my head while I was reading. I would come up for air hours later, in a bit of a daze. By the last hundred pages or so, I was racing breathlessly through chapters to get to the denouement. Not to say it's perfect. In the midst of all the excitement, my mind snagged on a few plot points that I found a little hard to believe, which I think is a real flaw in a mystery novel. I hate hearing that little critical voice at the back of my mind when I'm reading, especially if it's supposed to be escapism. It was also slow to get started. I knew from the synopses that she goes undercover, so why spend the first hundred pages setting it up? Let's go! My last criticism is that French indulges herself (or her narrator) sometimes by rambling on, but I think The Likeness is an improvement over In the Woods, in which you can skip entire passages and not miss anything important (although for the record, I am not usually a passage-skipper). 
 In a lot of ways, this book reminded me of Donna Tartt's The Secret History, although it doesn't benefit by the comparison. French's novel is more genre, less literary than Tartt's. Tartt's novel leaves you with a feeling of unease and corruption. I left the book feeling a little tainted just for having read it, which is pretty powerful. French's is a more conventional mystery, and not as well-written as Tartt's. For all that, though, it was a great summer read for the beach (or even for a long winter's night). I look forward to reading French's next.

 Rachel commutes daily on the train and she watches the people in their homes. She comes to "know" them through her train window. One day she sees something bad happen and she reports it to the police and this is where the story takes off. Prior to that, I wasn't sure how I felt about this book. I had a hard time connecting to the beginning of the story because it was very disjointed since most of it was told from a drunken pov. But once the incident happened and the reader starts getting clues to what is happening I was on board that train with Rachel trying to figure out all the secrets and lies. 
 If you like psychological thrillers then hop on board this crazy train where everything is either a secret and/or lie. 
 STANDALONE

I think the only good thing I can say about this book is that I bought it when it was on sale so I only wasted $0.99. It was slow, repetitive, and drawn out for way too long. The "twist" was not surprising. The end was completely unsatisfying. Just another story of dumb kids behaving badly. For the life of me I can't understand the 5 star reviews. I am obviously in the minority as everyone else seems to love it. Maybe if I had listened to the Serial podcast I would have appreciated this more? I did actually like the format, though, so I don't think that's it.

Kari is a young 16 year old schoolgirl who likes to keep herself to herself. 
 Whilst she's out walking home from school she meet the elusive Eddie. Now Eddie seems to be a bit of a movie star at her school, always giving presentations and talk sessions to young kids. He comes off as a respectable elder, little do we know he is a serious SLEAZEBALL 
 We see Eddie's actions as he seduces young Kari and eventually sleeps with this young "Virgin", bear in mind he's like 18-19. 
 Kari is on top of the world right now, that is until Eddie drops a bombshell.......He video tapped the whole thing! 
 We are then fast forwarded 2 years in the future and we learn just how much of a sleazeball Eddie actually is. 
 He demands money from Kari to keep his mouth shut. 
 This ghost of her past is still hanging on tight and will not let her go no matter what. 
 In swoops her saving grace "Neil Mars" As a reader I fell in love this character immediately! I mean how Rucy describes Neil in the book is HOT and you'll want him to swoop you off your feet and rescue you! 
 The sexual tension between Neil & Kari throughout this book is awesome, I freaking loved it. 
 As you can imagine though Kari tries her best to elude Neil in every way. 
 She's closed herself off from men, but for some reason Neil has gotten through her barriers, and it scares her. 
 Kari is a broken, fragile girl who needs to be loved the way a young girl should be loved, and there's no one better then Mr Neil Mars. 
 Rucy Ban's writing was packed full of emotions & flirtatious banter between the young love couple. 
 This book is Sexy, fun and passionate. 
 I honestly can't wait to read the second installment "Wear You Down", which is expected to be released November 2013

Didn't wow me like the first book did, but I enjoyed the character development with Lily & Rule & more Cullen time! 
 However I didn't enjoy the, let's call it the weirdness, that took up a good percentage of the book. I had trouble seeing how this moved the series along in some aspects but it does let you know, but not in the same way Tempting Danger did. Which I think was my problem as i preferred the first book! While there was a climax to the near ending of the book I felt a little let down with the actual ending. It was a little too neat and tidy for my liking but this could be because some of the next book has more to do with Cullen & his lady than with Lily & Rule (guessing from the blurb of the next book) but I could be proven wrong & a new storyline may feature. 
 Although not everything from Tempting Danger was wrapped up in Mortal Danger so the story arc may continue unless I'm over analysing! 
 Great to see a few new characters & some of the previous ones too! Looking forward to reading the next book & also worrying how things may develop!

This was a refreshing read for me in that I haven't picked up a contemporary adult fiction novel in a while. The book itself was kind of a mixed bag. 
 I didn't have any expectations going in. The story was interesting but not completely engaging. Quite a few moments seemed pretty far-fetched and really tested my ability to believe what was happening. I'm thinking specifically of Lotto's big incident at his prep school. (I had to put it down and then power through when that particular bit happened). Lotto as a character I didn't find that likable. I'm not quite sure how to describe it, but he's pretty frustrating. 
 Mathilde's history is intriguing, although the deeper it delved, the harder it was to suspend my belief (similar to Lotto's prep school incident). I liked her, but am conflicted with her portrayal and her actions to support her husband. She went without meals while he pursued a fruitless acting career and while he obviously loved her, he never recognized that. I know that's part of Mathilde's character, but it made Lotto a lot less likable. The 'contract' in her past was pretty troubling and I can't tell if the author was trying to make some kind of statement or if it was merely for shock (I feel it was more the latter). That sex scene with the sushi in his apartment was so...it just seemed incredibly unnecessary and very pandering to straight guy humiliation kink. I don't mind sex scenes at all, and there's obviously a lot of loaded and problematic things about that particular relationship, but JEEZ. It felt like the oddly descriptive stripper scene in Water for Elephants. It doesn't add the story, the character, and feels like it was inserted for the purpose of getting male readers off, honestly.  
 The writing was dense and thoughtful. A lot of reviewers said it was pretentious and I can definitely agree with that, but again, I enjoyed it if only for the fact that it was breaking up some of my reading habits as of late. Whether you hate it or you love it, it certainly sparks quite a lot of discussion. I also have to wonder if this was written by a male author, would it still be getting the same kind of criticism? Maybe. 
 I have heard compared with Gone Girl a lot, and from what I know of that novel, I don't think this is true. While I haven't read it, I feel like that's become a sort of tagline to get readers interested in the next big thing. This is a slower paced novel about a marriage between two people you don't think will make it work, but they do. One thing I liked about their marriage is that they never cheat on each other although Lotto came very close with his operatic friend, which I'm still surprised didn't actually happen . This may seem like kind of a stupid thing to praise, but marriage and adultery are represented pretty strangely in novels and films. I also appreciated Mathilde's ending. It's not something you see terribly often and I felt like that part of the book was realistic. It wasn't quite the happy ending most envision after tragedy, but it was real. 
 I don't know if I could really recommend this book. I'm glad I read it, if only to see what all the hype was about. Is it the greatest novel written? I don't so, but the writing was still very good, if a little pretentious. It's sure to make you think a little bit, if you love it or despise it.

I know I shouldn't introduce my own memoir with this amount of insecurity, but my personal life philosophy is always to assume the worst, then you're never disappointed. 
 I'm almost ashamed to admit this, but I haven't always been a fan of Felicia Day. It was pretty rough in the beginning, which for me all started with Dr. Horrible's Sing-Along-Blog. It wasn't until the death of her character, Holly, on the show Eureka that I started to warm up to her and examine what it was about her that I previously didn't like*. And then it hit me: I really just didn't like Penny (Dr. Horrible). As for Felicia? I am BEYOND cool with her. I mean, I feel like if I knew her IRL we would be BFFs. This sentiment was only strengthened and solidified through my first (yes; first, as in of many) readthrough of You're Never Weird. Plus, The Guild. And, duh, Charlie (Supernatural <3). I feel like I was just shocked and confused at our initial introduction and then was just completely thrown off guard while reading her book, like who is this majestic creature?! Life is weird and I apologize for any previously (completely idiotic and misguided) ill sentiments. Love you, Leesie! (Sorry) 
 But here's the part I unapologetically embrace: My weirdness turned into my greatest strength in life. 
 For the record, I have read her hardcover book (she liked my tweet about this and it 
 made my life 
 ) and listened to her read the audiobook (twice); both checked out from the library. Even if you've read a physical copy, I highly recommend listening to the audiobook. It just feels like chatting with or simply enjoying the company of a close friend while you're driving to work or gaming or however you enjoy audiobooks (and if you don't, again, I recommend giving it a try). I then also bought the paperback copy, because you never know when you're going to need to read this book again and why not have a copy on hand at all times? It's like having your best friend around all the time, but not in a creepy or annoying way. Or some better metaphor. 
 I've always felt like a failure inside if I'm not already a success. If that makes any sense. 
 Anyway, reading this book is wonderful, cozy, hilarious, and comforting on so many levels that I feel I simply cannot do it justice by putting how I fully feel into words. But I'll try. In many ways, I felt like I was reading my own inner dialogue. Her humor is smart, witty, and honest and the way she relates her life experiences and anxiety remind us just how human she truly is. As another reviewer so nicely stated, this isn't simply a celebrity memoir; this is a memoir that just happens to have been written by a celebrity. 
 Once you tell people exactly what you will and won't do, it's amazing how they'll adjust. Or they won't. And then an opportunity or relationship goes away. And that's okay. 
 As someone who is also weird, has anxiety, and dabbles in the World of Warcraft, I found her memoir to be hilarious, relatable, and inspirational. I know that Felicia doesn't necessarily like being dubbed "Queen of the Geeks" or other similarly hefty titles (it makes me anxious on her behalf to carry the responsibility associated with this), but I still can't help but feel that she is at least in some way deserving of our praise and admiration. Putting yourself out there, as she does throughout this memoir, and making yourself vulnerable is an incredibly terrifying, brave thing to do, regardless of whether or not (but also, maybe, especially if) you have anxiety. I feel a little bit guilty for saying this, but reading about Felicia's anxiety and depression helped me gain better perspective about my own anxiety and depression. And it made me feel at least a little bit better about myself, if only to know that I'm not the only one who has had those kinds of thoughts, feelings, neuroses. Misery may love company, but so does crazy...it's just too stubborn and self-conscious and overly analytical to admit it. For this, and so much more, thank you, Felicia. <3 
 I was born anxious. My mom must have watched a horror movie in utero or something, because I freak out at loud sounds, driving at night scares me because all the lights make me feel like I'm inside a UFO, and I'm traumatized, never delighted, by things that are startling. 
 Your qualification for finding a place to belong is enthusiasm and passion, and I think that's a beautiful thing. 
 Anyway, I loved her hilarious descriptions about things, particularly her inner dialogue when meeting Nichelle Nichols or...honestly? Everything. From her Introduction, wherein she meets and then accidentally offends some fans at a Build-A-Bear Workshop, through her Book Tour in Portland (all the coffee!), I loved every wonderful, awkward story. Please write more things, Felicia! Also, her Foreword was written (and read, in the audiobook) by Joss Whedon and, I mean, how cool is that?! I'm sorry, is my geekdom showing? Good. 
 It's hard being weird. No--it's hard living in a culture that makes it hard. -Joss 'The Boss' Whedon 
 *I thus completely related to Felicia when she was describing her therapeutic process of writing down ruthless things about friends and loved ones...only to realize she didn't hate them so much as something they had done or how they'd made her feel. I didn't (still don't! <3) hate her, I just disliked her character. I've rewatched Dr. Horrible since those days of my misguided youth and, actually, I can't even say that I feel the same way about Penny anymore, either. She's really not so bad after all (though she clearly should have been with Billy and not that tool, Captain Hammer *eyeroll*). 
 I wrote down everything I felt, including terrible things about people I loved, in order to move through and get to the TRUTH of what I couldn't see through my fogged state of mind...Working through my initial reaction always got me to understand what was really going on.

What can I say about Losing Hope? You know most of the time you go along reading books that you like, you rate them with 4 or 5 stars in your Goodreads account, then you hit a book that makes you cry, smile, and give you goosebumps. You sit still at the end thinking, "This is how books are supposed to make me feel." Yea, you know that feeling? That is Losing Hope. As a matter of fact, that was Hopeless, too. I loved Hopeless! This is Holders POV of Hopeless, however, it's not a rehashed male version of it. She didn't copy and paste and write in Holders name instead of Sky's name in this book. Its all new information that helps us understand Sky and Holders relationship, and also the relationship he had with his sister. All very important stuff that only helped make Hope/Sky and Holder the rich characters that they are. 
 I cannot stress enough that it is NOT a retelling of Hopeless. If you loved Hopeless, you will love Losing Hope. I am sitting at work finishing this book and have goosebumps and am holding back tears. Sad tears for what Sky, Holder, and Les had to go through to find their happy ending and happy tears because they find their happiness in the end.

I am kicking myself for not having picked up Vicious sooner. I knew it was well-received, but for some reason I thought the book would be boring. I'm not sure why I got that impression, but I was wrong, wrong, WRONG! Vicious was a complete and total page-whipper! 
 The book opens with a man, Victor, and a young girl, Sydney, digging up a grave. Quickly, we learn that this grisly task is all part of a mad scheme for revenge, years in the making. Victor has just broken out of jail. And he has one hell of a grudge against his old college roommate, Eli. 
 This decision to pit two former college roommates against each other is just inspired. In my experience, your relationship with your college roommate is one of the most intense and bizarre relationships you ever have. You're both "young adults," living in an oxymoronic state, under the influence of higher education, sleep deprivation, intoxication, and whatever the hell else you put into your system. Your roommate becomes in turn, your friend, your ally, your enemy, your obsession, your nightmare. V. E. Schwab deftly captures all of these dynamics that bounce between Victor and Eli. 
 Eli and Victor's vortex of envy and murderous loathing begins ten years before the current events of the novel, when they choose their college thesis topics. Victor chooses to study  adrenaline.  Eli chooses to research  ExtraOrdinary abilities.  The events that follow, during their spring semester of their senior year, are shocking. 
 Of course, Eli and Victor have back-up personnel to aid them. Two talented sisters, Sydney and Serena, find themselves on separate sides of the vendetta. And of course, Victor has his cell-mate and break-out buddy, Mitch. And there's the dog, Dol. All of these labels -- hero, villain, sidekick, mascot -- get tossed around and mixed up. Who is who? 
 These characters were all fantastic. I especially appreciated Victor. He was a highly complex character, but Schwab still managed to keep him consistent. I was at times, horrified by Victor's decisions, but somehow kept rooting for the man. I loved hating the self-righteous Eli. Sydney and Serena were used as effective foils to Victor and Eli's twisted brotherhood. I appreciated what it said about the nature of conflict that these two mirror-image sisters wound up on opposite sides of someone else's fight. And Mitch was a steady column of normalcy and reason that balanced the other characters out. These were fabulous players in a fabulous plot. 
 The pacing was also a strong point in Schwab's novel. The narrative flipped around in time, but this hardly phased me. At first, I had a preference for the present events over the past, but very soon I was fully engaged in the entire story, past and present. I was so absorbed in the book that at times I forgot that I was flipping paper pages and reading symbols made of dried ink. I was inside the story. What a rare and wonderful experience! 
 So, in short, I HIGHLY recommend this book. Five north stars out of five!

This review encompasses both this book and its sequel, The Wise Man's Fear with very minor spoilers (only in terms of references and not plot). 
 For me, Patrick Rothfuss has successfully created one of the best "coming to age / power" stories... ever. I won't summarise the plot here since many reviews have already done that, but I do want to to highlight a couple of (perhaps weird) details about Patrick's worldbuilding that made this book a total joy to read. 
 Money and gold does not fall from the sky 
 Richard and Kahlan walked Terry Goodkind's world seemingly with no care about how much travel or food costs. Erikson's armies do get paid some gold but without the reader having any clue whatsoever about how much that gold is actually worth in terms of goods / services. George R.R. Martin's scheming nobles are established in terms of being "rich" or "in hard times" but again with no real scale that the reader can use to measure a family's wealth. Even Lynch's Locke, despite being in essence a thief, get's away without the reader being worried about whether he has food to eat for the day. Infuriatingly, Potter's attendance of Hogwarts (and his clothing / food / equipment) is guaranteed simply on grounds of him being able to do magic stuff. 
 I absolutely loved the "hard" currency system of Rothfuss's world and the constant struggle of Kvothe to find the money to help him eat / attend the university / travel. Kvothe's ongoing battle to go from dirt-poor to ... relatively poor :) was such a really refreshing change. 
 You're the hero, but I can kick your butt easily 
 Yes, we're dealing with a coming-to-age/power story here. Yes, Kvothe is "special" but only in the sense that he was trained to be so. 
 No crazy inherent abilities that manifest in a time of need. No godly powers bestowed upon a successful quest. 
 Kvothe is a talented musician but you are reminded many times that far more capable musicians have graced the Eolian's stage. 
 He studies like crazy on the University to gain mastery of his powers and he appears quite cocky and successful at first, but he is not a god nor does he know everything. His peers will occasionally best him / teach him / remind him of his place. 
 He is determined to become a warrior yet he is beaten (thorougly) by a 10 year old. Not to mention the - excellent - scene where you expect him to reach one of the highest stones of the Adem only to see him being thoroughly pummelled on the 1st.  
 For Erikson fans: You know when you shouted "WTF, I want MORE! GIMME MORE!!!" when you read about Rake's visit to the Seguleh city? (couple of lines of text and a reference of martial prowess, that's it...) Until Erikson decides to grace us with a short story for that, Kvothe's visit to the Adem is the perfect fix for you. 
 I'm a noble, and you're dirt despite saving my daughter from the bad dragon 
 Another refreshing change from your classic "I'm-the-king-you-saved-my-daughter-I-am-indebted-for-life-and-will-make-you-rich" scenario. The Maer's attitude towards Kvothe (before and after) was priceless (pun intended). Yes, the hero will go forward to save the day but after all, he's not of noble stock, so let's not go crazy with admiration. 
 Why you should read these books 
 - Because Severen's "status rings" idea is the best I've come across in 15+ years of reading fantasy. 
 - Because Kvothe is at times a joy to follow, and at other times an annoying prat you're struggling to like :). Not as bad a some of K.J.Parker's characters but still. 
 - Because you know that eventually he makes it (after all, he is talking about his story) but you never really know how successful he will be or what he has sacrificed. 
 - Because Tabernaen and Imre feel like a proper cities and not a slapdash arrangement of (grimy / poor / rich) plot locations. 
 - Because "magic" is f***ing difficult and complex to do, and you get to appreciate that. 
 - Because fighting is also f***ing difficult to do, and you get to appreciate that. 
 - Because Kvothe does not "quest" to {insert dungeon / library / forgotten fortress / fantastical plot location} to find out about his arch-nemesis. He studies, he asks, he fails, he is constantly arriving on dead ends and the more he does so the more you get hooked on the story. 
 - Because on Erikson / Modesitt books when you encounter a poem or song you skip it as filler. With Rothfuss, even the silly children's songs make sense and have something to add. 
 - Because Sympathy is so much more complex and rich and difficult to do than Sanderson's Mistborn "push-metal-do-stuff" system. 
 I'm eagerly waiting for the third book.

This book is a tome! At 1400+ pages, it is the equivalent of four or five regular-length books. I don't know if that makes it a great value for the money though because I borrowed it as a digital audio book from my library. I'm spoiled by being able to get through a book in 1-3 days and this one took much longer. It created a log-jam for the other books which were on my to-read list and for that, it was frustrating. 
 This is the fifth book in the Outlander series. A lot of little, everyday things happened in this book but there wasn't a driving plot device at work anywhere throughout. I wasn't bored, but I also wasn't eagerly anticipating the next chance to read it whenever I had to put it down to live life. To use foodie terms, it was quite digestible but it wasn't delectable or gourmet. I could have read a few other books with a devouring interest in the time it took to get through this one. 
 I still want to read the next book in the series because I like the characters and want to see what happens to them but I don't mind waiting a bit and if it goes on and on like this one, I may lose interest in the series.
Thought I'd enjoy this more, but I just didn't.

Wow. Not only did I forget how much I loved this series, but THIS BOOK. I vaguely remembered bits and pieces from reading it five years ago, but now it's all slammed into me and I LOVE LOVE LOVE IT. 
 Welcome to the Glass City - AKA Alicante! This book is a bit different from the first two so far. It starts off with a bang and it just keeps going. There isn't really any down time. You are in and you are being pulled under by the current of this story. Needing more action. Wanting answers. Craving CLACE. 
 "There is no pretending," Jace said with absolute clarity. "I love you, and I will love you until I die, and if there is life after that, I'll love you then." 
 Out of all of the characters, this book broke my heart piece by piece for Jace. You can't help but feel sorry for him, and also, a little peeved. I'm not spoiling the book but, WHY WOULD YOU DO THAT, JACE? AND THAT? AND THAT? 
 I still love you. 
 I would like to take a moment and say just how much I love the scenes between Jace and Clary. They are filled with struggle and torment masked as a hunger that runs deeper than their bones. The development of friendship between Simon and Jace and the bonds growing between all of the other characters is also an awesome bonus in this book! 
 Off to book 4! :) 
 Rating: 4.5 stars!

I made a deal with myself that I'd read more Stephen King books after reading Carrie because I wanted to get to know this author more - to understand the hype and if he's really a great writer. Of course, I don't expect him to capture all audiences but I want to know if he's an author that I'd love. If Goodreads had a half-star system, this on might get a 4.5 from me instead. I ended up really liking the format of this book, but it took awhile to get used to and at times it confused me or I got slightly lost. Not very badly, just slightly. If you didn't know, this is a sci-fi action story that, instead of through narrative, it told through text messages, emails, surveillance reports, military reports, interviews, and a few images. And other formats I missed or probably can't quite describe. In any case, it is very different and for the most part it is pretty easy to read. I think what confused me were some of the more imagery-related text-- I read it out of order due to the way it was laid out. Also, when the formats changed for the same scene/event, I think the sudden switch caused me to lose some understanding. 
 I actually liked the plot much more than the characters in this one. Not that the characters are bad, but I think since again, the way it is told, you don't get to be inside the characters head and as such you don't get to know them as well as in some narrative stories. The plot was a little slow in the middle, but it really picks up fast towards the end. I read the last 200 pages in one sitting because I had to know what happened, and I was just so shocked at some of the events. I totally fell for Ezra being dead and that I thought Kady was going to die. I slightly spoiled the ending for myself while flipping through the book because at the end there is that image made of text of a girl and boy hugging and I assumed it was Kady and Ezra, and so I knew they get to be together at the end. But after AIDEN saying Ezra was dead and Kady being exposed to so much radiation I thought they were together in the afterlife. In any case I was like ohmygoodness this is a tragedy and I wasn't expecting it. I know it is a series but I thought at the time of reading the subsequent books would focus on the surviving characters and not Kady and Ezra. Honestly, I love Kady and Ezra together and living, but I would've been okay with their heroic deaths to propel the rest of the series. But again really happy they are alive and I get to read more about them later on. Also, the amount of death in this book was surprising. I was not expecting it to be so bloody and violent.  I won't say too much about the plot since I think its a good book for just diving right in given the format. There is a lot of stuff going on though and for a 600 page book it goes fast. You do have to remember there is a lot of spaces/images, etc given the format, so don't let the size intimidate you. 
 The book really gets 5 stars for overall design, except the plastic dust jacket was really annoying to read with on. I have OCD and always read hardcovers with the dust jacket on to protect the actual cover from skin oils, etc, but I had to take it off because it was just so slippery. It is really cool but not actually practical for handling while reading. Still practical for protecting from dust on the shelf though. :) 
 I'll be looking forward to the next book in the series, which I hope has a bright blue or lime green colored cover, because I think that would look awesome next to this orangey one. =)

So for the first book I have the read and unquestionable four stars but for the second Rebel Angels I have that one a three star rating. Why the drop? Isn't a series supposed to get better at you go along? 
 Well yes I suppose it it or it get steadily worse either way there is is some kind of consistency. 
 The funny thing about this series was that it was a little different in that respect. 
 I loved the idea of wild untamed magic controlled only by women, set against the prudish backdrop of the Victorian England. When a woman had to ask the permission of a male relative, who was in charge of her well being, if she so much as wanted to draw breathe, that was if she could breath thanks to her corset strings that where pulled so tight as to give her a more agreeable figure. 
 Hell I recently learned that there were even night corsets that women wore to bed!! Ridiculous! 
 Things start off not all that unusual, a whinny teenage girl bemoaning her lot in life because her mother wont allow her to go to England were it's fashionable, and then everything goes wonky with her mothers death and her witnessing it clear across from the other side of the town in India where she has spent all her life. The start makes you immediately sit up and take notice. 
 So she, Gemma Doyle, get her wish. Which puts one in mind of the saying "Be careful what you wish for." 
 There was so much about the male characters that rubbed me the wrong way through the entire series, even more so about the adults, even those that we only meet in passing. There is not a page where you are ever allowed to forget that women were not seen as useful, intelligent, unless they could make a lucrative marriage. No matter how old the women where they were spoken to, spoken of as if they were no better than toddlers. We are constantly told that that if a woman did not have the right title, beauty and the correct upbringing she better have money (well her father as women couldn't own anything) because without those things she wasn't worth anything and she would only look forward to a very bleak future. 
 We meet four girls that on the surface appear very different: 
 Gemma: she begins to discover that she isn't like everyone else. She is so much more 
 and neither is everything quite what it seems. The people around her are more 
 than what she ever though they were. Her mother has never been the perfect 
 perfect Englishwoman Gemma through she was. Her father has his own dark 
 dark secrets of addiction that come to light when he looses the love of his life. 
 Even her brother is more than what she thinks as she begins to realise what 
 his fears and desires are. 
 Pippa : beautiful, the perfect image of what a lady should be, wealthy, the perfect catch. 
 Or is she? Pippa holds a secret that if ever known will make her unmarriable. 
 This secret reveals that she is less then perfect, so her mother is in a hurry to get 
 her married to the most eligible man (which is code for wealthy) even if he is 
 fifty. But who wants to be sixteen and married to an old man. But what other 
 option does she have. 
 Ann: intelligent and gifted, but not ideally beautiful and to make matters worse, poor. A 
 scholarship who's fate is to become governess to her wealthy cousin's two 
 daughters. She is never accepted and constantly reminded about her position or 
 lack thereof. 
 Felicity: The leader of the four girls even though it is Gemma who holds all the power. 
 Felicity holds social influence. Beautiful, wealthy, willful, from the right family 
 and spiteful. She never lets anyone forget what her station is. But even she has 
 dark secrets of her own. And not just that her parents act if she barely exists or 
 that it appears that by book two she is jealous of her parents new ward. 
 The story of these girls reminded me in so many ways of Alice in Wanderland, in a world were everything is possible and where every wish and desire is at your fingertips why would you not want that power all the time. 
 The story for that Felicity creates the night that the girls first establish their secret club sets the tone for the entire series: 
 "Shall I tell you a story? A new and terrible one? A ghost story? Are you ready? Shall I begin? Once upon a time there were four girls. 
 One was pretty. 
 One was clever. 
 One charming, 
 and one...one was mysterious. 
 But they were all damaged, you see. Something not right about the lot of them. 
 Bad blood. Big dreams. 
 Oh, I left that part out. Sorry, that should have come before. 
 They were all dreamers, these girls. One by one, night after night, the girls came together. And they sinned. Do you know what that sin was? No one? 
 Their sin was that they believed. Believed they could be different. Special. They believed they could change what they were--damaged, unloved. Cast-off things. They would be alive, adored, needed. Necessary. But it wasn't true. 
 This is a ghost story remember? A tragedy. They were misled. 
 Betrayed by their own stupid hopes. Things couldn't be different for them, because they weren't special after all. So life took them, led them, and they went along, you see? They faded before their own eyes, till they were nothing more than living ghosts, haunting each other with what could be. With what can't be. There, now. Isn't that the scariest story you've ever heard?" 
 Having a taste for a power, beauty and choice in another world makes three of the friends, Ann, Pippa and Felicity hunger all the more for what they cannot have in their own world. In a way having been able to experience in small quantities but knowing that not only could it be taken away from them at any time but that without Gemma they could never posses the type of power she had makes them desperate and in someways even resentful. 
 Right through the series the girls never really seem to truly be friends, they are there is pettiness and the worse kind of nastiness. Ann is never even fully accepted by her only friends, and they seems to put her down at every turn. In a large measure Ann is also frustrating because she accepts this, even resorting to hurting herself so that she feels different type of pain. 
 Their open betrayal of Gemma leads to one of their numbers death but do the girls learn from their carelessness? No they don't. 
 One would think that by the second book even that there are so many people against them, so many forces seeking to tear them apart that they would learn to stand together in everyday and not allow pettiness and perceived slights to get in the way of their friendship but no they don't even learn that. 
 Gemma also seems less concerned about learning to really using her gift, and being able to bring it to bear than she is about trying to show everyone else that she is right even though her decisions keep costing her. And even the fact that she allows fears of loosing her friends approval leads her to keep doing things that she knows will probably end in disaster. 
 More back ground could have been given about secondary character which would have made the story a lot more interesting but that wasn't done. 
 I did like the introduction of Katrik to the story, I would have liked to have seen more of him through out all the novels. 
 Sadly I didn't finish the last book in the series, when the same issues keep cropping up it becomes annoying. In the first novel Gemma struggled to access the realms, second book same thing and in the beginning of the third book we are again faced with this as an obstetrical. I understand that Bray need to introduce the schools burned wing as the entry point for what needs to happen but I think she could have used different means of bringing it in. Then even after you learn so many things about the girls they're back at one another's throat from the get go. And once again her friends selfishness is what causes problems and Gemma's stupidity and compounds things so I ended up closing the book at about chapter five or six in disgust. 
 On the whole I'd give the entire series a 3.

I was too young to remember this being a news sensation in 1994 and I'd never heard of Yummy's story until I picked this up. Tragic and intimate, Yummy is told from the perspective of a neighborhood boy who watches as his classmate gets inducted into a gang, mistakenly kills an innocent girl, and is then killed by his own gang to put an end to the media attention surrounding the police search for him. Sadly, more than 20 years later, this story is still relevant. 
 Each year it seems Chicago hits a new record for gun violence and gun related deaths. As of today, November 5th, 2016, Chicago has seen 3,733 shootings and 632 homicides since January 2016. That is insanity. And that is just one city. When violence on that scale becomes part of daily life and daily news, it's easy to lose perspective and to stop understanding it on an individual, personal level. That is exactly why books like Yummy are so important, no matter what age you are. Behind every statistic there are at least two human lives, one on either side of the gun, to say nothing of the friends and family left to cope or the children who grow up with this as their norm. The other thing Yummy does so well and with such subtlety is show what a complex issue it is. It extends beyond "getting guns of the street" (though that's important) to addiction and an overall lack of opportunity and resources. We need books like Yummy to force us to take a closer look and to show us that it's not so cut and dry. 
 This would be a great text to use in a classroom but really I recommend it for anyone. It's not a long read and it's an important issue. If you watched The Wire and are still devastated when you think about Bodie, Poot, and Wallace, read this book.

An interesting examination of how education alone isn't the answer, how being brilliant and gifted doesn't matter. Even being hard-working, that greatly extolled American virtue, didn't save Robert Peace, who died in a drug-related shooting after a stellar academic career took him from a rough neighborhood in inner-city Newark to Harvard. I've read some reviews that seem to hold Peace at fault for not leaving his community for a high-paying research job in some Research Triangle suburb. I think it's unrealistic and hard-hearted to expect someone to leave their family and their community behind for success in a mainstream, mostly white world. Peace's story made me think of Ta-Nehisi Coates article, The Case for Reparations and how even if a person of color is successful, the likelihood that their intimates are not makes it more difficult for them to determine their own destiny (for more on this, listen to Brian Lehrer's interview with Coates here. He talks about this problem explicitly around the 18 minute mark.) Coates explains that individual achievement and success is no match for living in a plundered community with little social capital to give their children the boost that the mainstream takes for granted. Leaving those larger questons aside, in Robert Peace's case, leaving the community he grew up in would be a betrayal of part of himself. Ultimately, I found the author problematic. Hobbs is straight-forward about his limitations understanding the world Peace grew up in, and he definitely tries his hardest to empathize with Peace and to grapple with large questions of the entanglements of race, poverty, drugs, and crime. But there are some cringe-worthy moments nonetheless, and too much emphasis on his own search for purpose and success. It matters who tells these stories, although I guess it's an improvement that they're being told at all.

Several of my high school students have told me that this is their favorite Dessen title, and they've read them all. Annabel is a protagonist every teen can project herself into - minor family problems, conflicts with sisters, mother who doesn't get her, a job she doesn't like, has a secret, at times socially connected but at the moment feeling isolated. I enjoyed Dessen's practical approach to these issues, not seeking to solve them completely, but to make their management a reasonable goal. 
 Annabel's new friend, Owen, is particularly enjoyable. He's a little angry, a little obsessive, and a music geek, but likable and completely noble. Instead of saving a damsel in distress, in true 21-century fashion, Owen mentors the princess so that she may save herself. 
 My problem with the book comes from not being the audience Dessen writes to. While the high school girls will eat this up, I (middle-aged man) found it tediously obsessed with explaining every nuance of every character's relationship with every other, and Annabel was so tentative that I struggled to care about her. For thoughtful coming-of-age/teen-problem novel without the melodrama of Ellen Hopkins this is good stuff.

Three books in one. All three novels begin with conventional set-ups (mostly detective noir) and then totally confound them. Basically, male protagonists, who aren't what they seem, get involved in spiraling investigative cases, often involving their doppelgangers. With pauses for cloud-watching, writing in red notebooks, and impersonating bums. And Auster includes loads of literary references (now I want to read Don Quixote), meta-fun, and existential questions. 
 The second volume, Ghosts, is my hands-down favorite. A slim, darkly funny, and experimental entry, it has the extra wordplay challenge of the characters' "colorful" names and shifting identities. 
 City of Glass is not without its charms with a gripping beginning and some inventive religious bits. It's also a lovingly rendered portrait of gritty NYC, replete with walking tours. However I hoped it was going to go to darker, stranger places. 
 Auster gets there in the last entry. The Locked Room contains the most violence and misogyny of the three tales, dishearteningly so. The final few pages attempt to tie the whole trilogy together somewhat. Struggling and failing with these unraveling threads seems to be Auster's point here: 
 "It as if Fanshawe knew his final work had to subvert every expectation I had for it. These were not the words of a man who regretted anything. He had answered the question by asking another question, and therefore everything remained open, unfinished, to be started again. I lost my way after the first word, and from then on I could only grope ahead, faltering in the darkness, blinded by the book that had been written for me. And yet, underneath this confusion, I felt there was something too willed, something too perfect, as though in the end the only thing he had really wanted was to fail--even to the point of failing himself (307)."
I enjoyed it, and it was very interesting but not as good as I thought it would be.

 Ahh, Franzen...we meet again. You quickly skyrocketed to the top of my favorite writers list after I read The Corrections. I continued loving your writing through the various essay collections you wrote in the decade before Freedom came out and I really liked that as well, if not quite as much as the Corrections. Which brings us to Purity... 
 First of all, the cover is a mystery to me and has to be one of the worst I've seen in some time. However, you know what they say about a book and its cover. The novel itself is quite entertaining and incredibly well-written. The problem is that the various sections into which you divide the novel and the characters in each one don't entirely mesh well. Your protagonist remains somewhat of a blank to me, even though I feel like we get to know her fairly well. 
 Your other characters come across much better, even if the second most central one, Andreas, is pretty insufferable. I also enjoy your Luddite-centric rants, even when others call you "Grandpa Franzen". I guess my main point here is that as good as this novel was, I wanted to like it even more. Others might complain about your portrayal of most mothers as being domineering and miserable, and they might even have a point that female characters are not your strong suit. I'm not going to hold that against you. I just wish there was more there there with this novel. Your characters don't have to be likable all of the time but you might want to make them at least a teensy bit more sympathetic.

From the Goodreads summary: "A boy drowns, desperate and alone in his final moments. He dies. Then he wakes, naked and bruised and thirsty, but alive. How can this be? And what is this strange deserted place?" 
 HAHA, joke's on you if you thought this book would ever actually tell you! 
 Patrick Ness's More Than This is what would happen if Alice in Wonderland met The Matrix. It's a ridiculous, otherworldly adventure never backed by any kind of satisfying explanation, and to add insult to injury, the adventure is a rip-off of The Matrix instead of an original fantasy like Lewis Carroll's. Seriously, someone needs to do a side-by-side comparison of lines from The Matrix with lines from this book, because I swear some of the ideas and even the dialogue are lifted straight from the movie. The high degree of similarity goes beyond just being inspired by an existing story and applying that broad story in a new way. It's straight-up copying. It's lazy, and it's bad writing. 
 So yeah, this book plagiarizes a movie so popular that pretty much everyone will be able to recognize the plagiarism. My bigger pet peeve, though, is the book's open ending. 
 As a kid, I never got all the hype about Alice in Wonderland. To me, it came across as a rambling, illogical dream. There was no way for me to get a solid grasp on the rules of the universe: what was allowed to exist in this world? where were the boundaries of possibility? It was just one random thing after another instead of a coherent story with a coherent setting. 
 In More Than This, it's pretty much the same deal. Just when you think everything's been explained as a less interesting version of The Matrix--just when you think you know what's real and what's not--you find out you're wrong, and then the book ends. 
 Ambiguity is really hard to pull off well. It can be really thought-provoking and poetic, but when done wrong, it's less poetic and more just frustrating. It feels like a cop-out. Like Ness wanted to write this epic scenario but couldn't think of a good way to explain why it would've come about, so he just didn't bother with explanations. 
 On another note, I noticed some other reviewers complaining that the book starts out slow. I can see why they'd say this. It comes across like I Am Legend without the pet dog or the threat of monsters. It's just one guy all on his own, foraging for supplies and sleeping a lot and exploring abandoned places. There's a lot of detail about what kind of clothes he finds to wear, what he eats for every meal, and so on. That kind of day-by-day survival story is totally my jam, though, so I actually really enjoyed it and felt that it was a lot more believable than the action-adventury, cliffhanger-every-other-page stuff that followed. 
 I have to give Ness kudos for a few things. I love that Seth (the protagonist) is gay but that it's not his whole identity. It's handled very well. And I love the brief but wonderful way Ness developed Seth and Gudmund's romance through flashbacks. I shipped it. Most of all, while I can't say I adore Ness's writing by any means, there were moments that were really perfectly done. One early scene in particular stands out: Seth is returning to his empty house after wandering around the city, which seems to be totally abandoned. As far as he knows, he's the only person in this whole world. He goes inside the house, turns on his flashlight, and: 
 The torch has caught the stairs. It's the first time he's properly looked at them, the first time a proper light has been on them, and he sees-- Footprints. In the dust coming down the stairs. He's not alone. There's somebody else here. 
 My skin crawled with how creepy that moment was. If the whole book had held that kind of jolting immediacy and emotional power, my rating would've been a lot higher. 
 As it is, there's not much I can say to recommend this book. It's my first foray into Patrick Ness, and I have to say I'm disappointed. It's mostly poorly-developed action sequences, plagiarized sci-fi, and unanswered questions, AKA pseudo-depth that made me wish I was reading a print copy instead of the eBook so I could throw it at the nearest wall.

I really wanted to like this book more. I admire Gilman enormously: a woman flouting society's values in turn of the century America was no joke (see House of Mirth). She thought, wrote, and lectured about women's place in society, its relationship with economics, and the crushing unfairness of it. It's inadequate to say she was ahead of her time, because her ideas helped shape our time. Her strength in defying convention to create a life that made *her* happy is an inspiration. Her utopia is less so. It's heavy-handed and boring. I had a literature professor who said that everyone reads Dante's Inferno and no one reads Paradiso because conflict is what's interesting. Paradise is boring. Also in this case, very creepy. Herland is a sterile monoculture and all that homogeneity gives me the creeps.

The Boy in the Suitcase has everything I normally look for in a good thriller: a strong, likeable and driven protagonist; a creative yet plausible plot; lots of action and suspense; and a setting which allows me to do some armchair travel through the vivid images of foreign lands evoked by the author/s. 
 Nina Borg, a nurse in a Red Cross Centre in Copenhagen, is a voice for the city's forgotten and unwanted people, especially the many Eastern European women and children immigrants who find themselves in trouble, either in abusive relationships or trapped in the sex trade in order to remain in the country. Her total absorption in her role has caused some trouble between Nina and her husband, who feels that Nina is neglecting her own family whilst trying to save the world. But when Nina receives a panicked phone call from one of her oldest nursing friends, Karin, to pick up a parcel for her from a locker at the city's main train station, she is again unable to refuse to come to the rescue. The contents of the locker shock Nina - a small boy, naked, drugged and zipped into a small suitcase. Fearing the worst and unable to contact Karin, Nina soon finds herself on the run with the child, hunted by the people who want the boy back. 
 This Scandinavian thriller, set in Denmark (and Lithuania), contains all the enjoyable hallmarks of its genre without being overtly dark and depressing. The authors skilfully explore the atmosphere of modern day Copenhagen and its problems whilst providing some hope by introducing a strong female protagonist who fights for justice amidst despair. I wholeheartedly liked Nina, and could relate to her on many levels. As a modern day woman she struggles to juggle family with career and marriage, whilst trying to make a difference in the world, a balance which is often her undoing. In her quest for justice she stumbles across the path of dangerous individuals and not only has to fight for her life but also for everything else she holds dear. 
 Having a nurse as protagonist, rather than a policewoman or PI, gave a completely different angle to the story and provided a refreshing change from your normal murder/mystery/thriller. Introducing each of the novel's characters with a separate, seemingly unrelated, chapter in the beginning of the book whetted my appetite to find out more and kept me reading until late into the night, until the threads all came together to form a violent, thrilling and surprising conclusion. In the course of the book the authors introduce several strong, interesting women characters, who drive the story towards its finale. However, I also liked how the "badies" in the novel contained a strong human element, which allowed for compassion despite their dangerous and dark sides. The authors insightfully explore each character's motives for their actions, grounding the story and giving the reader the opportunity to see each person as a three dimensional human being. As a nurse, Nina is also able to remain empathetic at all times, displaying her need to help and nurture in a very surprising act towards the end of the book - which I won't give away here. 
 I thoroughly enjoyed this novel and am looking forward to reading more from this dynamic author-duo, Lene Kaaberbol and Agnete Friis. Highly recommended - 4.5 stars.

Here, we are first introduced to sophomore Reed Brennan, a scholarship student at a prestigious boarding school in Connecticut, and her attempts to socially climb her way up and into Billings House, the elite dorm for upperclass girls who "go on to do great things." Reed hopes to eventually make it into Billings (enter hazing tactics here) in order to rise above her home life, where she has left behind a sweet and devoted father along with a hateful, alcoholic mother. Within months of starting at this school, she goes from failing to acing her classes (thanks in large part to genius Taylor; Billings girl), dating the most popular senior, Thomas Pearson, to dumping him (wait...did he just disappear? Gossip!), and gaining an "in" with Noelle and her group of the Billings girls. 
 I get that this is an "elite" boarding school experience, where most of us could potentially relate to middle-class Reed, but any connection to this character or the story gets lost along the way. Between the severely flawed and one-dimensional characters, most especially naive and wishy-washy Reed herself, and the plot that tries to be several stories at once, there is simultaneously too much and not enough happening in Private to entice me to continue with the series. And I am not one to simply stop reading a series, no matter how terrible it is (looking at you, L.A. Candy). Oh, well.
